speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask the Minister of National Defence this question. Has the minister received a communication from the attorney general of the province of British Columbia requesting the assistance of the army in the East and West Kootenay areas for the Doukhobor problem?

speakeroldname: Hon. D. S. Harkness (Minister of National Defence):
subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO REQUEST FOR ASSISTANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday afternoon I did receive a telegram from Mr. Bonner, the attorney general of British Columbia, the material part of which read:
Would earnestly recommend Canadian army immediately station appropriate units in the East and West Kootenays for practical training in army's current domestic role.
People in Kootenays and government of British Columbia would welcome federal co-operation of this nature as complementary to efforts of provincial and municipal enforcement agencies now fully engaged in this area.
Following receipt of this telegram I telephoned Mr. Bonner and pointed out to him that it was apparent that the reason he wished troops to be stationed in the Kootenays was that they might aid the civil power. I stated he should follow the regular procedure as laid down in the National Defence Act, sections 218-228. Section 219 in particular reads:
The Canadian forces, or any unit or other element thereof, or any officer or man, with materiel, are liable to be called out for service in aid of the civil power, in any case in which a riot or disturbance of the peace requiring such service occurs, or is, in the opinion of an attorney general, considered as likely to occur, and that Is beyond the powers of the civil authorities to suppress, prevent, or deal with.
This section and the others referred to place squarely on the attorney general of the province the responsibility for requisitioning military assistance if, in his opinion, it is required. I assured Mr. Bonner that if assistance was requisitioned in the manner laid down by law, it would be provided in a matter of hours. I further advised Mr. Bonner that in my opinion I had no authority under law to send in troops to assist the civil power unless they were called for in the circumstances as laid down in the National Defence Act.

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO REQUEST FOR ASSISTANCE
speechtext: A supplementary question. Does this in effect mean there has to be a state of martial law declared before the minister sends in troops?

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO REQUEST FOR ASSISTANCE
speechtext:
There is no such thing as a state of martial law, as I understand it.

The National Defence Act is clear. If military assistance is required by the civil authorities, the procedure is clearly laid down; they' request the nearest army commander for that assistance, and he is obligated under the National Defence Act to supply it.

Mr. Chairman, last evening for a considerable length of time we were treated to some remarks by the hon. member for Niagara Falls which I must say, as minister, I found gerry-waring-excuse me, I mean very wearing on the credulity. The remarks which were made in two separate interventions in the debate by the hon. member occupied almost an hour and were filled with inaccuracies, innuendo and allegations. I should like to deal this afternoon for a short time with some of those allegations. I think I should refer, first of all, to the remarks of the hon. member as recorded on page 1728 of Hansard:
-I have never before in my life seen such an obvious and barefaced collusion.
I submit, Mr. Chairman, that the hon. member probably knows more about collusion than about tenders and business practices, because the one tender submitted displays what I regard as the most flagrant and obvious example of barefaced padding of a contract that, in my business experience, I have ever encountered.
There were several remarks made by the hon. member with which I should like to deal, and the first of these has to do with the employment of one Mr. Paul Brett, who is now employed as a forester in the Indian


affairs branch of my department. Mr. Brett, it is true, was in the employ of Mr. Johnson to whom the hon. member referred. This employment terminated on March 31, 1961. However, Mr. Brett had, a month or more previous to this time, made application for the position of forester with the department, under competition properly advertised by the civil service commission.
I am told that there were a dozen or more applicants for the position. He won the competition, taking the examination in the usual course under the civil service commission. As hon. members of this house are aware, in this case the department accepts the person who is selected by the civil service commission. Mr. Brett was then appointed to the staff of the Indian affairs branch. He took up his employment with the branch, not as the hon. member says on April 1, but on May
1.	This is one of the inaccuracies which have been built into the story the hon. member produced for our edification last evening.
There are other matters with which I should like to deal as I come to them. For one thing, the hon. member made the allegation-I suppose that is too broad a term to use; made the statement-that Beaufort Industries did certain things. I find it very difficult, in jumping around through this speech, to discover which Beaufort company she is talking about, because I find there was a Beaufort Industries incorporated in 1958. I do not know if this company discontinued' its activities, but it was taken over by Beaufort Holdings in January, 1962, a full month after tenders had been called for this timber. Then a new firm, Beaufort Industries, was incorporated on January 19, 1962. We have, therefore, Beaufort Industries No. 1, Beaufort Industries No. 2 and Beaufort Holdings. I presume we can assume that in the first part of her remarks, when she is building up her story, she is referring to Beaufort Industries No. 1. Then when she starts to talk about the ultimate tender which they submitted she is talking about Beaufort Industries No. 2, which was finally incorporated on January 19, 1962.
However, to return to her statement, I find she is reported on page 1725 of Hansard as saying:
At this point I might say that Beaufort Industries Limited is a company of all Canadian directors and shareholders, located in Vancouver, and has been cutting timber for a long time in the Tsimpsean I.R. No. 2 reserve, in the reserve area, and cutting it very successfully.

I wonder if I might interrupt the minister. I had risen to make certain corrections in Hansard, but the hon. lady had started her statement. I had not said last evening they had cut timber in this reserve,, but near it. If the minister wishes to make

her statement prior to my being able to make those corrections, then I would like her to know she is referring to things that were inaccurately reported.

I accept the correction, but I was about to declare that I know of no basis for the statement that Beaufort ever cut timber on the Tsimpsean reserve No. 2, and I might say further that the department has no record of any previous dealings with this company in respect of any Indian timber.
There are several other points to which I would like to refer. As reported on page 1727 of Hansard the hon. member said that the advertisement which was inserted in the newspapers calling for tenders had been changed to read "February 13", and that no notification was given to the Beaufort company. Well, Mr. Chairman, I have here two newspapers, the daily Colonist of December 22, in which the original notice calling for tenders was advertised, and the following day's edition, December 23, in which a revised notice appeared in the same paper extending the date. This was the only notice that was given to any tenderer and it was obviously well known to Beaufort Industries, as it was to the other companies which were interested in this tender; because in the intervening period between December 23 and January 19 representatives, or let me say a representative, of Beaufort Industries was in my department on several occasions and referred to the fact that the date had been extended.
I might direct attention further to the fact that had the original date been adhered to, up to that time Beaufort had not even received consent to their ultimate incorporation. Undoubtedly the extension of the date benefited them to a greater extent than anyone else. This extension was made in response to the suggestion of our officials in Vancouver, who had received representations from several persons who allegedly were interested in submitting tenders, drawing attention to the fact that one month was scarcely sufficient time for them to prepare and submit their tenders.
As recorded on both pages 1727 and 1729, the hon. member also referred to the fact that Beaufort had tendered on some 8,000 acres of timber which were not included in the tender of the successful tenderer, and the question was asked why we put up only 4,760 acres for tender and excluded the other 8,000 acres. The 4,760 acres contains 85 per cent of all the merchantable timber on the reserve, amounting to 160,500 hundreds of cubic feet. The 8,000 acres referred to is
13, 1962	1739
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration mostly marsh and rock and contains only about 15 per cent of all the merchantable timber, amounting to 24,000 hundreds of cubic feet.
Quite apart from the fact that this area was hardly worth logging on a commercial basis, it was considered that the timber on it could well be reserved for future logging operations by the Indians themselves, if and when they wished to do so. I might also say that in this submission presented by Beaufort, quite apart from the fact that it included these 8,000 acres, the tender contained a clause in their proposed contract which would allow them to withdraw from the extra 8,000 acres if the timber proved unsuitable for operation.
Perhaps the hon. lady will admit on this point that it would be only with the department's permission?

Why include it in the tender in the first place and then, as I said before, pad the tender price up to make it look like an attractive offer on the basis of something which they were subsequently to attempt to withdraw? It seems to me, talking about red herrings, this one is at least slightly pink.
Now, there was considerable discussion with reference to the construction of a road and some other matters that were included in the tender of Beaufort which were not stipulated in the call for tenders, and accordingly not quoted on, by the other tenderers.
Any company which engages in lumber operations must build roads to carry out its purposes. Of course one company may build a road in one direction and another company may build one in another direction, and if it turned out that the Indians would like to have a road built in a direction other than that which might have been indicated by another tenderer, then of course that would be taken into consideration.
I might say that I do not intend to pursue this matter because I believe it is one that should be discussed by someone who is familiar with the terrain which, as I understand it, is a very difficult part of the country stretching from the place where logging operations would take place to the head of the inlet. Whether or not a road in that particular locality would be of use to the Indians is a matter on which I am not qualified to judge. I understand that at present there are no vehicles there. In the long run there may be, but there are none at the moment and, as nearly as I can calculate by looking at the map, the road to be constructed would cover a distance of some 15 miles.
The hon. member also referred to what she called the stunning regularity with which Mr. Johnson's and Mr. Brett's names came up. I might say that she herself certainly made
1740	HOUSE OF
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration a point of repeating these two names throughout her tirade last evening, but she referred to Mr. Johnson as an employee of the department. On more than one occasion she used the phrases "when he left the department" and "a former employee." Mr. Chairman, Mr. Johnson was never an employee of the department.
Oh, oh.

The firm of which he was a principal tendered along with some eight other firms in 1958 to provide a survey of certain forest potentials in British Columbia. He was the successful tenderer, as he had been when he was previously engaged by the department of Indian affairs under the former regime in 1956. At that time I understand there was no public call; it was just two firms which were asked to submit tenders, and Johnson's firm submitted the lower of the two quotations. I would suppose, Mr. Chairman, that since this company was engaged by the former government, that proves that their reputation and integrity is above reproach.
Oh, oh.

Consequently when they won the subsequent tender in 1958, in competition with seven others, I can find no particular reason to quarrel with this arrangement.
Another statement was made by the hon. member which is reported at page 1727 of Hansard. She said that Beaufort had been advised that it had won the contract as high tenderer. Now, Mr. Chairman, this is not exactly the case. As a matter of fact when the tenders were received, as is usually the case the tenderers had representatives present, and at that time Beaufort were advised that it appeared they had submitted the high tender but that both tenders with their supporting documents would have to be examined before a decision could be made. This is just slightly different from the hon. member's version.
I must say in all honesty that throughout the remarks which were made there is just enough semblance to the true facts in many cases to make it very difficult to say "This is wrong, and this is right". This matter of whether or not they were told they had won is a very good example. The hon. member's words were, "They were told they had won the tender", whereas the actual words that were used were that they had obviously submitted the highest tender but that the various tenders had to be examined before a decision could be made. This is what makes it so very difficult to draw the line in all these allegations and statements which have been made.


Mr. Chairman, the hon. member had quite a bit to say about a number of things. She said, for instance, that last autumn an offer was made in writing by Beaufort in the amount of $791,000, and she wanted to know why it was that this amount was so close to the successful tenderer's amount of $792,000. As a matter of fact no such tender in a specific dollar amount was made by Beaufort. Under date of August 11 they wrote a letter to the department and offered to purchase at $7 per thousand. Someone else has done the arithmetic which arrives at $791,000, but no such amount was mentioned then or subsequently by them as a dollar amount for the offer which was made.
The hon. member has also said that she wanted to know why it was that the tender call said it would not necessarily accept the highest or any bid. Mr. Chairman, anyone Who has had a great deal of experience with tender calls knows that this is pretty standard form. It was, however, a form which the Beaufort company chose to ignore by sending in a submission on an entirely different basis and one which, as I have said before, served to pad their price to an almost unrecognizable degree.
That means the Indians would get more.
Not necessarily.
Then what does the hon. lady mean by "pad the price"?
I will tell you precisely what I mean by that before I finish. As a matter of fact I see no reason why I should not tell you right now-
I think it is a good idea.

-because if you add to
the bid of Shoreline of $792,000 the 30 cents per 100 cubic feet which was offered for the training plan, you get $792,000 plus $48,150 or $840,150. They had not included this amount in their tender, but Beaufort did include the amount, and they did not include the amount at 30 cents per 100 cubic feet. They showed the cost of training at 50 cents per 100 cubic feet. They also included the 20 cents rental per acre-

Would the hon. lady confirm this point? The Shoreline bid was for $6,000 a year and the Beaufort bid was for a maximum of $20,000 a year, or $200,000. That is the difference between 30 cents and 50 cents.
I am afraid I do not understand the hon. lady.
I am sure there is a difference between $60,000 and $200,000. The hon. lady is supposed to be an accountant.

Yes, I was supposed to be, and that is why I get so confused with these legal statistics which seem to be so much at variance with those which are accepted common business practice. To go back to this matter of the evaluation of the two tenders, I have now given the committee the figure by Shoreline, with the training plan, of $840,150. If you take the bid of Beaufort, their stumpage amount is $631,950, and you add to that their estimate of the cost of their training plan, which is $80,250, and possibly the hon. member will realize that in putting in the $80,250 as against the $48,150 of Shoreline I have recognized the differential which she mentioned. Then you add to that the rental of 8,000 acres at 20 cents per acre which they submitted as a contract, amounting to $16,000 and you still only get $728,200 as compared with Shoreline's $840,150. As I said before, the rest is padding.
That is, the roads and planting are the padding; is that what the minister is saying?

I will come to that, too. I draw to the hon. member's attention that I sat quietly last night and listened to her for nearly an hour. I made one or two small interventions which I thought were pertinent to the debate. I think perhaps she should contain her soul in patience until I finish.
Hear, hear.
I shall try to do so.
Take your medicine; it is free.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: It is not very hard to take.

It was also said that the contract for Shoreline was on a one year basis. Again this is wrong. The contract was on a 10 year basis. I fail to understand where this one year came into the matter, because the contract was exactly the same for both companies and each of them contracted for 10 years. So all this reference which creeps in here two or three times is wrong. As a matter of fact it must have been sold to the Indians too, because I see it is in their resolution which mentions the one year, whereas the actual term is 10 years.
The hon. member referred to the resolution which had been submitted by the chief of the band. I might say that this resolution did not come to me; it was sent to the Prime Minister, and I secured a copy of it. But apparently at the same time it was sent to the Prime Minister it was also sent to the hon. member, who in that event had it before I did. It seems
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration to me that if action is expected the resolution should be sent to the head of the department concerned, but apparently this is a new system. In any event, of the first three items which are now asked for by the band, none were in the call for tenders.
Shame.

It seems to me I heard the hon. member say "shame". Possibly I should point out to her that the officials of my department consulted with the chief and with the band before the original tender was put out, and the terms which the chief of the band required to be in the tender were placed in that tender. These other matters have been raised not only subsequent to the calling of the tenders but subsequent to the eventual consideration of the bids. In other words they are an afterthought.
I submit that a story has been very carefully built up here for the purpose of creating a false and distorted version of the facts. Unfortunately this false version appears to have sold to the Indians. The fact is that the general terms of the call for tenders were, as I said a moment ago, worked out with the members of the band council. They made no reference to the building of a road between Tuck inlet and Fort Simpson. The question of the road is therefore outside the terms of the tender. This having been said it should be added, I think, that whichever bidder is awarded the contract will be obliged at his own expense to construct a suitable network of logging roads in order to get the timber out of the area. I mentioned this earlier in my remarks this afternoon, and it is a fact well known to all foresters and logging people.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. I regret to interrupt the minister, at this point, but I must tell her that her time is expired.
Carry on.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I see it is the wish of the committee that the hon. lady should continue.

Thank you, Mr. Chairman. I might as well do this all at once instead of in two parts.
This area cannot be logged in any other way, and the cost of logging roads should properly be regarded as part of the cost of operation, not as part of the price paid to the Indians. As a matter of fact, the remark was made in an offhand way by one forester who had taken a look at these tenders that if the Indians took the extra $160,000 which they would get from Shoreline they could build the road themselves.
The call for tenders did not include a requirement to replant the area which is to be cut, for the reason that the timber cruise
1742	HOUSE OF
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration report for the area in question stated that the area would regenerate its own forest cover by natural means, and that artificial reforestation was not necessary. I am told that the problem in this area, because of the heavy rainfall and so on, is to stop the trees from growing, not the replanting of them. It is true that replanting is engaged in in certain parts of the country and in connection with certain types of logging operations, but I do not propose to go into that matter now because I do not think I am any more of a forestry expert than the hon. member for Niagara Falls is.
There was a reference to the fact that the call for tenders included only 4,760 acres as against the extra 8,000 acres. I have already dealt with this, but I just might add that the Indians themselves were aware of that fact at the time the call for tenders was put out. The timber cruise report made it clear that there was very little marketable timber on the 8,000 acres and that this parcel should not be included in the call for tenders. I said this a few minutes ago but I repeat it now because this was a fact which was well known to the band members.
I might just make a brief reference to the concluding part of the resolution which was received from the band affirming the band council's refusal to accept any tender which did not conform to the four stipulations laid down. My only comment on this is that if these were to be essential features of any successful tender they certainly should have been stipulated in the call for tenders before it went out. We can hardly justify calling for tenders on the basis of one set of criteria and then awarding the contract on the basis of another set.
So in order to clear the air-because it certainly is well fogged up now-I should like to say that though the Indians were consulted on the details of the original call, they now appear to be dissatisfied with the terms on which that call was issued. As we know, they have now listed four conditions in their council resolution, three of which are new. The fourth does not apply. There is the term dealing with the requirement of a road from Tuck inlet to Fort Simpson; that dealing with reforestation which, I have said, is not considered necessary or even desirable in that area, and finally the extension of the area to cover 12,620 acres instead of 4,620 acres.
As I said yesterday in reply to a question on orders of the day, and as I repeated last evening, immediately I received word of dissatisfaction with the awarding of this tender, some ten days ago, I gave instructions to the department to have the commissioner in British Columbia visit the band in question
[Mrs. Fairclough.l

to discuss the matter with the chief and his band members. I may add that in the meantime I have received conflicting reports from a number of people in British Columbia with regard to this matter. I have had two reports from Indians, some from people engaged in the forest industry, and others from persons otherwise interested. They do not all point to the same conclusion.
Therefore I agree with the hon. member for Vancouver East, who said last night that he thought it would be a good idea to get this whole thing cleared up as speedily as possible. I think he is quite right; the issue is certainly well befogged now. So in view of this and in fairness to the Indians, who are after all the owners of the timber, we have no alternative in my view but to cancel the original call for tenders and the bids relating thereto and start all over.
Hear, hear.
That is the best applause I have had from the opposition since I have been in this post.
Remember when you cancelled your immigration regulations?

This is what probably would have occurred in any event. I am still awaiting a report from the commissioner on his return from the reserve. As hon. members familiar with the area will know, this is a remote place. It is difficult to get into. The commissioner probably would have been there last week had conditions been suitable for travelling to that part of the country. He is there today, I understand, and I expect to have a report from him when he has ascertained the wishes of the Indians, and this time we had better get them in writing. We shall then, I expect, if the Indians wish it, issue another tender call with specific stipulations. The tenders which will then be received will be considered on the basis of the conditions set out by the Indians and incorporated in the tender call. If there is further padding I can assure the committee that we will have to slice it away once more in order to arrive at comparative values.
Nevertheless, as I said last evening, although this particular item is not properly included in the supplementary estimates which are before the committee for consideration, I am pleased to have had an opportunity to present to the committee as much information as is presently available. I admit this is probably not the whole story, and I do not think the whole story will be known until we receive the report from the commissioner on his return from the Tsimpsean reserve.
I do not think, though, that I need to apologize for the consideration which I have

given to the affairs of the Indians. They have never lacked a sympathetic ear when they have come to me as bands, as associations or as individuals, and they never will lack a sympathetic ear as long as I hold this portfolio. 1 do not claim 1 am the only person in this chamber who is sympathetic toward the Indians or who is concerned with their welfare. I am sure that practically every hon. member is also concerned that the Indians should receive a square deal, and that is what we try at all times to provide for them.
This tender call has resulted in a flare up, and the whole issue is beclouded by charges and countercharges which I do not think are particularly good for the final resolution of the problem; nor are they good for the Indians themselves or for the trust which they must of necessity place in those who are attempting to administer their affairs if the best of conditions are to finally evolve for them and their children.

Mr. Chairman, I roundly applaud the minister for her decision to cancel the contract as let and to call it again at the desire of the Indians. This is in keeping with the highest traditions not only of many things the minister has done but also with the traditions which are required of a member of the privy council and particularly a person responsible for the trust with respect to Indians.
Last evening and again this afternoon when the minister commenced her remarks I was somewhat startled by the vehemence with which she attacked the address I made last night. I explained last evening that I was raising this matter as one of urgency, although the minister indicated she did not wish it done. I felt it important to raise the matter because I felt there were a lot of facts that should be placed in the possession of the minister before this investigation concluded.
I rose at the beginning of this debate to attempt to correct some of my remarks as they appear in Hansard, and I should like to proceed to do that at this time. Some of them are erroneous, and I regret the fact that when I reached the debates office last evening it had closed.
At page 1725 of Hansard of March 12, in the left hand column, approximately half way down the page, in the paragraph beginning with the words "within a matter of two weeks" the following sentence appears:
He suggested that negotiations be conducted directly with the superintendent and the bands and chiefs council-
That phrase, of course, should be "chiefs and band council".
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration
In the right hand column on page 1725 about halfway down the page the reference to "Indian superintendent" should be "Indian commissioner".
In the lower right hand column on page 1725 the reference to Beaufort Industries Limited as a Vancouver company should be corrected to indicate that it is a Victoria company.

Mr. Chairman, on a point of order, there is a proper place and time in the proceedings of this house for an hon. member to make corrections. This is not the proper place for the hon. member to attempt to correct her remarks-
She can make corrections at any time.

Just a second. Sit down and be quiet. Let someone else finish his remarks before you interrupt. The hon. lady should wait and make her corrections at the appropriate time. When orders of the day are called she should stand up and make corrections-

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Don't be afraid; she will stand up.
I point out, Mr. Chairman, that the hon. member has already had an opportunity to do that today.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I believe the corrections the hon. lady is making relate to the debate now proceeding, and since reference has already been made to some of these comments I shall permit her to proceed.

Thank you, Mr. Chairman. The following is the phrase to which the minister referred. At the bottom of page 1725 in the right hand column I am reported as having said that the company has been cutting timber for a long time on the Tsimpsean reserve. Properly the word "reserve" should be dropped out because it was in the reserve area. While the minister indicated that the department is not aware of the company doing any work in the area, it did in fact recently complete a Masset operation in the Queen Charlottes, very close to this land. It was a very successful operation, well known in British Columbia forestry circles.
In the upper left hand column of page 1726 where I refer to Mr. MacGregor as the acting superintendent, the reference should be to acting commissioner.
In the lower right hand column of page 1726 I am reported erroneously as having said there was a call for tenders made on September 15, 1961. That should be "December" as is reported further along in the paragraph.
One final correction-

Supply-Citizenship and Immigration

Perhaps the hon. member would permit me to interject an observation at this point. I do not wish to interrupt her corrections, but with regard to the last correction she mentioned she said the call was sent out to Beaufort and to another company. This was not correct. The call was in the newspapers. It was not sent only to individual companies. It was a public advertisement.

With reference to that, the minister may be advised that I was informed that a call had been received through the mail. I was so informed yesterday by an official of the department. I was informed that it had been sent directly to individuals who had been writing the department and who were interested. I was informed there were individuals who got it through the mail.

That is true, but it was a public call advertised in the press, as distinct from a call sent to specifically selected individuals or companies. As the hon. member has now said, it was sent to more than these two companies. That would be only common courtesy when companies had been making inquiries with respect to a given project. They would, of course, be notified if and when public tenders were called.

This was the point I made earlier, that they did in fact receive the call with a specific date by which tenders were to be in, on January 13 or January 16, and they were not notified by mail of the change. The change only appeared in the printed advertisement in the newspaper.
Yes. The change appeared in the printed advertisement in the paper; no one was notified.

One other correction. At page 1728 in the upper left hand column I am reported as having said:
In fact it should be remembered that Mr. Johnson-and Mr. Brett had been associated with Mr. Johnson-
That should read:
In fact it should be remembered that Mr. Brett- and Mr. Brett had been associated with Mr. Johnson-
I do not understand that correction.

The statement which reads that Mr. Johnson-and then there are dashes -and Mr. Brett had been associated with Mr. Johnson should read that Mr. Brett- and then following the dashes-and Mr. Brett had been associated with Mr. Johnson, the chief forester of the Vancouver office.
At page 1730 there are two substantial errors. In the right hand column at about the middle of the first solid paragraph I am recorded as having said:
I would suggest to the minister that notwithstanding what I am advised by the department-
If I did in fact say that I was in error. It should read:
According to what I have been advised by the department-
As it appears it completely reverses the sense of what I meant to say.
Further down in that column I am reported as having said:
It was Beaufort that brought to the attention of the department a fact that anyone who obtained foreshore rights would in fact be giving the Indians access ultimately to the ocean.
The word "giving" in that sentence should be "denying". So much for the corrections.
There were also a number of suggestions by the minister to the effect that I had attempted to colour the evidence which I put before the house. There were her references, including that to the employment of Mr. Brett, who it appears now was employed a month later than I had indicated to the committee. The information about the date of his employment was supplied to me by an individual in the Indian affairs branch to whom I spoke yesterday just before coming into the house. If it is in error, I am sure that it is his innocent error and mine as well.
What was his name?
I do not think it is necessary for me to give it. I believe the minister knows who it is. There is no secrecy about it.
No, I do not know.
It is a matter of no importance, in any event.

On the question of Beaufort's incorporation, may I say that I am not a solicitor for nor in any way associated with Beaufort. However, I had made inquiries with respect to this matter and I am informed that the company's solicitor believed that the company would not have sufficiently wide objects and therefore a reconstitution was made in the company in order to broaden its objects. At least in so far as I am concerned it appears to have no significant importance, and appears to be a matter on which the minister was grasping for straws in trying to answer the suggestions which I put forward last night.
As to the question of why 8,000 acres were excluded and only 5,000 acres were put in the offer, as I think I pointed out, in 1954

and 1956 the department saw fit to offer all of the land; and as the minister told us frankly this afternoon it was because of the cruise report which was prepared by Mr. Johnson's company for the department that only 5,000 acres were offered. I was told yesterday that it would appear ridiculous if the government were to offer the whole area. They now know they have someone who wishes to purchase the whole tract. It would seem to me that what they have been told by a number of individuals who are experienced in forestry is that if in fact all the timber is not offered at once, the Indians will never be able to sell it because it is not economic to go into such rough terrain to take it out, and it will just remain there.
Who are these experts?

The reference with respect to roads is, I think, an important matter, as it is obviously of great importance to the Indians. I have not visited this reserve. Perhaps the hon. lady has done so. However, it is apparent from the maps that it is just south of Alaska. Bad weather prevails much of the year. In fact the successful tenderer has indicated that there may be a time when he will not be able to carry on any operations up there. I am informed there have been at least some Indians who have died when travelling off the coast on the way to Prince Rupert, which is the northern settlement. This will give them a real safety factor, and is something which ought to be considered.
I do not for a moment suggest that Beaufort, in saying that it would spend up to half a million dollars in building such a road, is doing this out of sheer kindness of heart. It is a logging road. It is for the purpose of their operations, which they think it would make more efficient. But it would appear that it would be of great and lasting benefit to the Indians of the band. In the alternative, the road offered by Shoreline was a three mile road which it was alleged could be built for $50,000 and which comes in from the Big Bay area, right through into a stand of better grade timber.
Whether the minister thinks there is any difference between a $50,000 offer and a $500,000 offer, I do not know. However, the Indians appear to feel that there is some difference. I believe such a road would be something which the Indian affairs branch will never build itself because of the terriffic cost. I am informed that a number of individuals in the department, both here and on the west coast have repeatedly said that such a road could not be built, and yet the minister has just said that someone else has said that the extra $160,000 offered by Beaufort could
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration be used by the Indians to build their own road. The department itself has said it could not be built. Mr. Beaufort has put engineers in and taken aerial photographs.
No, that was not said at all.
The minister did not say this. I was told this by a representative of the department yesterday.

No. If the hon. member will permit me to say so, I think what was said was what I said earlier, namely that it was difficult terrain and it would be difficult to build a road in that area. However, I do not think anyone at any time said that it could not be built.

That was the suggestion made to me yesterday. Again, with respect to replanting may I say this. The minister goes back to the cruise report, and I appreciate that this may be all the department has. But sight should not be lost of the fact that the cruise report was prepared by the Johnson company, that is the company which is owned by the man who was the successful tenderer under another corporate name. Of course it will cost him and every other timber man in the whole of the west a considerable amount of money if it became a standard practice to require replanting. Every timber man who went in to cut on Indian land or any other land then might be required to replant, and it would cost several million dollars a year. There is reason to say that no one who is in the lumber business on the west coast wants a requirement that there be replanting. This is an important offer as well from the point of view of employment of the Indians because, as is apparent, elderly people, those who are not particularly strong, women and children could be used in planting seedlings, and not just able bodied men.
There is another matter to which as yet no reference has been made. I refer to the number of people to be employed. The successful tenderer says that he will employ in the first year only 10 Indians, and that when he is fully going he will employ 20 Indians out of 32 men. The Beaufort plan indicated that they would employ about 100 Indians. That makes a considerable difference in the wages paid to and the skills learned by the Indians on the reserve.
Yesterday the minister said something else about which I meant to ask her last evening, but there was not time in which to do so. She said that before March 7, which was the date of the resolution, she had ordered an investigation. I do not think she favoured the committee by telling us the reason. This tender was opened on February 13. On February 21
1746	HOUSE OF
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration Beaufort was advised by telegram that it was the lowest tenderer. From February 21 to March 7 nothing appears to have occurred.

If I may answer the questions as we go along I think we might save time in the long run. Earlier in my remarks today I explained that matter, when I said that upon receipt of information to the effect that the Indians were not satisfied, I then ordered an investigation.

There is one other matter to which I wish to refer. The minister has said she is going to recall tenders. As I said before, I think this is an excellent idea. It will be to the satisfaction of the Indians, who are really the only people concerned or the only people with which this committee need concern itself. However, the minister made some slighting reference to my humble experience with tenders. I have had some experience at least as a municipal solicitor. Certainly in my remarks yesterday I pointed out that it was usual to have a clause providing that the department may refuse to accept one or the other or both. However, I suggest to the minister that if she wishes to avoid what she calls padding, certainly one of the most important things is also to avoid conditional tenders, that is tenders which are called and which are accepted should in fact be proper tenders which are unconditional. I agree with the hon. member on that point.

There is one other matter I should like to mention. I hesitate to try to lecture the minister, but the letter which was produced yesterday, and about which the minister made a most offensive suggestion that I might have removed something from the files of the department-
I never said any such thing.
Perhaps I am being oversensitive.
I think I just asked if it was on the files.

When I was reading from a photostatic copy of the letter the minister asked, as reported on page 1725 of Hansard:
May I ask the hon. member from what document she is reading?

"Gleaning" is removing.

Of course no such thing happened at any time. However, the letter does indicate a rather shocking condition, Mr. Chairman, and that is that this man Johnson, on the letterhead of the company which was appointed as a consultant to the department-
Under contract.

That is right; but on the same letterhead this Mr. Johnson offered, on May 30, to peddle this information. His work had been completed on March 31. If the minister has not seen this letter I shall be happy to send it across to her.

I have not any particular spies out who are trying to find letters which may come from persons who at one time or another were under contract to this department and who subsequently pursued their activities with other industrial corporations.
While I am on my feet, Mr. Chairman, I might say with respect to the 100 Indians that I never at any time saw this information given by letter, by word or in any proposition, from the Beaufort company. This is the first I have heard of any offer to employ 100 Indians.

There is something else about this letter. In my opinion it is rather shocking that anyone could be employed by a government department, get information and then go out and sell it. I know that some of the people with whom I have been talking on the west coast have gone to the Indian affairs branch on the west coast and have been told it is the Indians' information; it

is not a public record. Here is a man who is getting paid more than $4,000 for this particular timber cruise-

You will note that the letter is signed by Mr. Johnson. Now, he is selling information which he had obtained. I do not know whether he becomes a civil servant or whether there is any sort of secrecy imposed when one becames a consultant of a federal department. However, it is one of the most reprehensible and shocking breach of confidence I have ever seen. Here is someone who has been paid out of public funds and then tries to peddle the information elsewhere. This is the reason, I suppose, for the fact that in the lumber industry in both the United States and Canada it was being said all last summer that Johnson would wind up with this timber; when Johnson was trying to obtain United States financial support to help him exploit the Indians.
I am delighted that the minister has seen fit to let air into this matter; that she has seen fit to cause an investigation to be made, and that she has assured the house there will be a recall for tenders in compliance with the desire of the Indians. I would only ask that when such tenders are called they be unconditional tenders, and that the department be scrupulously careful in looking at those who are tendering to ascertain who they are, what their experience is and whether or not they have information, privileged information from departmental officials or otherwise.

Mr. Chairman, this is a most interesting document which the hon. member has read into the record. However, it does not alter the fact that there is no such thing as a direct scale arranged between a firm of consultants and the superintendent and the chiefs of the bands. Any such transaction must, of course, pass through head office, and it would normally be handled in the proper fashion. Surely the hon. member does not expect the department or the minister or the government or anyone else to decide what are proper business ethics and at what time information gained in the course of fulfilling one's contract with another department or a department of government, should or should not be used.
But in so far as the information being secret is concerned, I might tell her there is no secrecy about the information gained by the Johnson company in pursuance of its activities, which I reiterate it carried out under contract won from seven other tenderers. There is no secrecy about it at all. These findings were published and were public knowledge. Anyone can get this information, and since it is available to anyone I suppose the company itself would think

Supply-Citizenship and Immigration it had a right to use this information. Certainly we have no way of policing the activities of these companies. I am not competent to judge whether or not this is a breach of business ethics, but in any event I would be pleased to see that the hon. member's views on the actions of the company in question are drawn to its attention.

I listened last night to the remarks of the hon. member for Niagara Falls, and I was shocked at the manner in which she endeavoured to smear the names of two respectable citizens in the city of Vancouver. She mentioned the name of one Thomas Ladner as a director of Shoreline Lumber Limited, and she went on to say that Mr. Ladner was "the son of one Leon J. Ladner"-
I did not say "J". I did not know that.

-whom she described as follows:
-who is probably known to many of my hon. friends opposite as the chief fund raiser of the Conservative party in Vancouver.
Well, Mr. Chairman, he is not known to me as that. In the first place I want to point out to this house that Thomas Ladner is a respected lawyer in the city of Vancouver. He is a man who had a distinguished career in the navy in the last war. He was highly decorated, and he has served as a police commissioner in Vancouver. He is a man whose name I believe it worthy of me to clear of any imputation made against him in this house. Mr. Ladner telegraphed me this morning and said:
X read this morning the report by Bruce Phillips of the Province Ottawa bureau of a charge allegedly made by Judy LaMarsh, M.P., concerning a company having the name of Shoreline Lumber Ltd., and advising that I am a director of that company. This is to advise you that neither I nor any member of my family ever had or will ever have any interest in this company. I hold my directorship in a purely professional capacity in the same manner as such qualifying directorships are held by me in dozens of other companies. I do not follow the business affairs of the company. No representation to any department of government in Ottawa was made on behalf of the Shoreline company by me, Mr. L. J. Ladner, Q.C., or any member of this firm.
I think that sets that record straight.
Now, as to the allegations of professional misconduct-and that is the only thing I can term them-made against Mr. F. J. G. Johnson, I shall not deal with them too fully. However, let me point out the fact that for many years Mr. Johnson has earned his living as a professional consultant forester in British Columbia. I might add that in British Columbia about 92 per cent of the forests are owned by the province. We have


many professional foresters now practising in consultant capacities who previously worked for the British Columbia forest service. They have gone into private practice and, by virtue of the knowledge gained by them when working for the British Columbia forest service, they have been able to make quite a decent living. In some cases former members of the British Columbia forest service are now senior executives of large companies, and I do not think anyone would suggest for one minute that they should not make available to their companies the knowledge they gained of the forest resources of British Columbia when they were employed by the forestry service.
So far as these various bids are concerned, I shall not waste too much time dealing with them, as the minister has stated that new tenders will be called. But I have taken advantage of the minister's offer to review these bids, as did the hon. member for Niagara Falls, and I may say I have had quite a bit of experience in examining timber business sale tenders. Having done that I must emphatically tell the house that in my opinion the bid that would have given the greatest net return to the Indians from the sale of this timber was made by Shoreline Lumber Limited. That is my judgment based on what I can ascertain by looking at the tenders which the department was kind enough to show me. Their bid was $792,000 for the timber and the comparable bid of the Beaufort company, as nearly as I can analyse its complicated tender, amounts to $516,000. In other words there is a difference of $276,000 in net dollar return to the Indians.
Perhaps the Beaufort company did undertake to build a road to Tuck inlet which the Indians might think would be of some residual value to them, more so than the roads which the Shoreline company would build. However, I submit that for $276,000 the Beaufort company could afford to build many, many miles of road on that reserve and in that area. In fact no matter how I look at it, having examined the tenders I come to the conclusion that the Shoreline bid was a better bid for the Indians than the Beaufort bid.
Much has been said about the Beaufort company's training plan. Well, any company working on Indian reserve timber and which under the terms of its contract is required to employ as much Indian labour as possible, is going to be concerned about a job training program. In its own interest it will be concerned to see that those Indians working for it are well trained. As a matter of fact there is no reason to believe that the Beaufort company would have instituted a training plan that would have provided any more for the Indians than that offered by the Shoreline company.

So far as reforestation is concerned, perhaps I am a little ignorant about the coast of British Columbia. I only happen to have lived all my life there and to have logged in almost every area of it. I notice the statement has been made that reforestation is urgently required up there, or words to that effect. The government of British Columbia are very concerned about reforestation under the sustained yield policy. I do not believe they have ever planted a tree in the provincial forests along the coast north of Alert bay. There is no need for it; God and nature do the job much better than man can. The real problem of reforestation up there is that after a number of years the regrowth is so thick that what it actually requires is thinning. Therefore if the Beaufort company had really been sincere in their concern for the future of the forest on this reserve and the future welfare of the Indians, they might have left a few hundred thousand dollars to be paid to the Indians for thinning at some future date.
Is my hon. friend suggesting that these 8,000 acres, which on one hand we are told are just scrub, do not need replanting?
No, they do not.
I doubt whether anyone, even the hon. member for Niagara Falls, could successfully grow trees on that so-called scrub area.
I am not about to try.
The soil conditions are such-
Don't underestimate her.

Mr. Chairman, I would remind the committee of the line in the old poem, "Only God can make a tree". The addition of this hypothetical sum for reforestation that the Beaufort company used was padding. There is no question about it; they padded up their bid. The figure of 60 cents per 100 cubic feet, or approximately $1 per thousand feet board measure, is just trying to kid the troops; it is trying to kid the Indians and the departmental officials, but I do not think the company was successful in doing that. I think in their negotiations with the Indians some representatives of this company have been speaking with a forked tongue. As far as the roads used for the actual logging operations are concerned, there is no reason to believe that the residual value of the roads left by one company will be any greater than the residual value of the roads left by another.
To come back to these 8,000 acres upon which the Beaumont company placed a value, from the best information that was available

They asked to have the area included in the licence for which they were applying together with the other 4,000 acres. All they undertook to do was to pay an annual rental of 20 cents per acre on these 8,000 acres -
If the department approved.

Mr. Chairman, I think the hon. member ought to be honest-
Oh, oh.

This company placed a fictitious value on their bid wherein they undertook to take over these 8,000 acres and pay an annual rental of 20 cents per acre per year until such time as they decided whether or not to take some timber off the area, if there was any commercial timber on it. If there was any commercial timber on it they assumed they would get it for the upset price they bid for the timber in the area that had been advertised.
I do not think the department would have been wise to agree to this sort of proposition, because they would have held that timber for 10 years under the terms of the contract, and at the end of 10 years, if they

Supply-Citizenship and Immigration did not decide to log it, they would have left it as it was when they acquired the licence. If they did decide to log it they would have had the full benefit of the stumpage value of the 4,000 acres they acquired; and who knows, five years or three years later the timber on those 8,000 acres, while today it is not considered to be merchantable, might be worth twice as much per thousand board feet as the timber on the 4,000 acres now being considered. I have seen that situation occur many times in my experience on the coast of British Columbia.
A number of other remarks were made concerning this timber. It was suggested that this was going to provide easy access for the Indians to Prince Rupert. It is not quite as easy as it sounds, because they would have to travel across a neck of land and then leave their boats at the head of Tuck inlet, which I do not think they would choose to do. A great deal was made of the fact that they had to go out on stormy waters. The Indians have been going out on those stormy waters for generations, for thousands of years, and usually the only time they have suffered a mishap was when they had been to Prince Rupert and were on the way home.
A charge of collusion was made in this committee last evening. The hon. member made it plain that she was not charging collusion against the minister, but she implied collusion of the officials of the department with outside interests. It is very clear to me that the basis for the compaint the hon. member has been making is the fact that departmental officials refused to enter into collusion with the people for whom she is acting as spokesman in this chamber, in refusing to sell this timber on a direct sale basis. That seems to be the whole basis of this complaint, that the department refused to sell this timber to the Beaufort company as a direct sale. To my mind the term collusion could properly have been used if they had agreed to sell this timber as a direct sale to the Beaufort or any other company.

In all fairness, Mr. Chairman, I should like to repeat what I said last night-perhaps the hon. member did not listen-and I say it again today; that I am not acting for anybody. I have no connection with any of these companies. In my view the two bids should have been rejected and a new tender called for. That is still the position I take. There are only one or two questions I should like to ask to conclude the matter.
Would the hon. lady allow another hon. member to have something to say?
I should like to ask the minister why it is necessary to have an export licence for such timber.
That is not a matter which comes within the ambit of my activities. That is a matter for the Department of Trade and Commerce.

I fully realize we have spent some three and a half hours on this subject, but in view of the statement made this afternoon by the minister in charge of Indian affairs I should like to make a few comments.
First of all, I can assure the minister that we in this group are most happy that she has found herself in agreement with the proposition that we tried to promulgate in the space of only ten minutes last night when we submitted that this was such a serious question that it should be clarified and handled immediately in an appropriate manner. We are therefore very happy that the minister has adopted our point of view and informed the committee that in view of all the circumstances she has issued a cancellation order with regard to the entire situation. The old tenders will be cancelled, new ones will be drawn up, and these, I presume, will be in specific terms so that anyone who tenders in future will have to do so on the strict basis of the tender.
May I express regret, however, that the minister did not undertake to do something which I still consider to be essential. Even though she has announced the cancellation of everything that has been done in the past there is still an odour of the past which has to be cleared away. In order that this may be done I strongly believe that a much clearer explanation should be forthcoming as to the manner in which the Indians would have got greater ultimate benefit by the acceptance of the bid on the basis of which this tender was previously awarded. The minister spoke for almost an hour, but I can assure her it was difficult to pinpoint any part of her remarks which might have conveyed that information. How would the Indians have received greater benefit by the acceptance of the one tender as compared with the other? I still believe that this has not yet been made clear, despite all the minister has said. There is still a nasty smell there, and it has to be cleared away. I sincerely hope it will be.
The hon. member for Niagara Falls, when she rose to ask a question, probably had the same thing in mind as I had. I remember what the hon. lady had to say last night in her contribution to the discussion of this important subject. She said that on one of the tenders appeared the statement that the terms were subject to the obtaining of an export

licence. That is matter which in no circumstances comes under the jurisdiction of the hon. lady. I cannot understand how any tender can be marked in that way, let alone be accepted by the department. That is matter which comes within the jurisdiction of a certain council in British Columbia and, I think, of the Department of Trade and Commerce. I do not remember the minister making any reference to this important aspect. Why should there be a tender containing that provision?
Mr. Chairman, perhaps I may be allowed-

I shall be very brief, and the hon. lady can reply all at once. I do feel strongly that something has to be said here. It has not even been intimated so far, but I think it had better be said. There is rapidly increasing belief, based on a growing volume of information in the last 24 hours, that what has basically caused this turmoil, this problem, is a fight between two companies, the Beaufort Industries and the Shoreline Timber Company, and that behind it all is party patronage-one Liberal and the other Conservative.
No Liberals at all involved.

One Liberal and one Conservative. This might just as well come out into the open. I do not know why it has not come out before, but I am going to say it. This is what is behind it all-the receiving of timber rights, the receiving of cutting rights which, in the final event, comes within the jurisdiction of a government agency. This might as well be said, and if the hon. member for Niagara Falls has not heard it or does not know it, then I do not believe it.

On a question of personal privilege, there has been some suggestion by the hon. member that he does not believe I have not heard such suggestions. I have, in fact; but as I assured the house last night there are no members of my party concerned with either of the companies as far as I am aware. As far as I am aware, the two individuals connected with the Beaufort Company are still at least nominal supporters of the hon. lady's party and not of mine, and I know of no individual involved in any way who is a Liberal.

I am surprised at the hon. member getting up in that way on a question of privilege. I said that this is the situation as it has come to my attention. I have such high respect for the hon. member for Niagara Falls as to believe she is not so naive as to state what she just did.

I think the hon. lady has done a service by raising this question. I hope others to the best of their knowledge have been able to do the same. I will go this far. If the minister had not made the announcement she did at the conclusion of her hour long statement this afternoon I was going to urge the house to refer the entire matter in all its complexity to the joint committee on Indian affairs of the house and Senate. I hope it will be made clear in the new tender that its detail, meaning, limits, operation and method of handling are to be free of political considerations so that no one can point a finger at anyone in the civil service charging that political activity occurred with respect to a matter affecting the Indians who come under the charge of the people of Canada through a department of government represented in the House of Commons by the hon. lady.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to thank the hon. member for his remarks. I must say I agree with him. I also agree that conditional clauses are not a good thing. I do not condone this and I am sorry it happened. I can assure the committee it will not happen in the future. Hon. members will realize, of course, that these calls are prepared and go out. They are not the type of

Supply-Citizenship and Immigration detail that necessarily comes to the minister's desk. My intervention in this matter occurred only alter protests were raised.
We shall try to make it clear to the Indians what the situation is so that they will understand the matter. I agree with the hon. gentleman that this is basically a fight between two companies. It has been attended by a great deal of, let us say, extracurricular activity. Lobbying methods, publicity methods, and so on, were employed, but that is the usual thing. With regard to the hon. member's charge of political considerations entering the question, I must plead innocence. Possibly I, too, am naive but I did not even know who were the principals of these companies until the protests were lodged. I still do not know who the principals in the companies are. I know only the names that were mentioned in the debate last evening. I suppose it would be possible to find out by writing to the provincial secretary and asking who are the directors of the company but I do not think I would do that-
You can ask your own office in Vancouver.

I have not had an opportunity to do that, of course, although if I wished to do so I could call the Vancouver office by long distance telephone. However, I would prefer to judge this thing on an objective basis and it is on that basis that I propose to take the action I indicated previously. I hope the final outcome will meet the satisfaction of hon. members of the committee, in the first instance, but that primarily it will be in the interests of the Indians.

Mr. Chairman, before this matter terminates there are a couple of points I wish to raise. I do not wish to deal with anything that has happened but there are a couple of points that trouble me about what may happen notwithstanding the very wise course the minister has decided to take in this matter, and I commend her for taking it.
One point concerning which the minister did not enlighten us-and this was dealt with in the remarks of the hon. member for Niagara Falls-is the question of what the status of the department is vis-a-vis the Indians, whether there had been a surrender and, if so, what the nature of the surrender was, and if not, why not.
I was not here yesterday and have not had time since reading Hansard to examine the statute and see what the statutory provision is. Perhaps the minister could tell


me immediately what it is. My recollection is that it would be possible to make a contract for one year without having a surrender but not for a longer period. However, that may not be the case.
Whatever the legal situation is it seems to me that before any attempt is made to make any contract with a new contractor a surrender should be made or, if a surrender is not necessary, a resolution should be adopted in very precise language. That language should be embodied in the tender call and strictly adhered to in the matter so that there would be no ground whatever for complaint or misunderstanding. I suggest to the minister that that be done before any attempt is made to call for tenders from anyone.
The second point I wish to make which in my opinion is also very important is that the minister cannot satisfy me and I do not think she can satisfy any member of the committee by saying that export permits are a matter for another department. The minister is a trustee for the Indians and she should not have asked for a tender before clearing up the matter of export permits in her capacity as trustee for the Indians. I do not know why export permits are necessary and I must say I was rather surprised to hear it. Surely timber is not a strategic commodity and surely it is not in short supply in Canada. There may be some quirk in the act or it may relate to some provincial regulation that the federal government is seeking to enforce although I doubt whether any provincial regulation would apply to an Indian reserve. I think the minister ought to clear up the matter and tell the committee what the situation is.
It is really perpetrating a fraud on the Indians and on the contractors to suggest that they can make contracts to cut timber for export until they know the terms and conditions under which it can be done. It is not good enough to say it is a matter for some other department when the minister ought to be dealing on behalf of the Indians with that other department to make sure that a contract of this nature can be carried out.
I am not seeking any answer from the minister now. What I am doing is recommending that before the matter is proceeded with further this question be completely cleared up and that it be indicated in the tender call that the timber can or cannot be exported, and by whoever is successful. If the Department of Trade and Commerce is going to be allowed, if it has the power, to discriminate against one tenderer as compared with another, that is a pretty state

of affairs that ought to be cleared up before any transaction of this kind is undertaken. There were implications that there might be something in that which I hesitate to believe, but it is not good enough to brush it off. I know they do not act like it but hon. members opposite are supposed to be members of a government with collective responsibility. In this instance I suggest strongly to the hon. lady that she act like a member of the government and not like an independent power.
The third point is that I do not think anyone can feel very happy after listening to the letter read by the hon. lady for Niagara Falls. It is quite true, as the minister said, that when I was minister this firm was retained. It is also true that since the present minister took office this firm was also retained. I have no criticism of either of these things because there is nothing in connection with either of them to my knowledge that anyone could criticize, but it does seem to me to be extraordinary conduct for someone, immediately he has completed a contract, to provide information which other people seem to have been told was confidential information-
Mrs, Fairclough: Published information.
Well, if it was published information why did not the hon. lady correct something-
I did. I already said that.
The minister said that the information was published?

I said the information was published. Perhaps I should not use the word "published". It is public information. It is available to anyone who asks for it and it is public knowledge that this information is available.

I must say I did not understand that from what the hon. lady said. If that is the case, of course, that quite alters the situation. However, I did not understand that from what I read of the debate last evening. I tried to listen attentively today. No doubt the hon. lady noticed that I was endeavouring to follow her remarks closely. I was really quite concerned about it. If the information is equally available to everyone, that alters the situation. However, it seems to me that it is still likely to create a bad impression for someone, the moment he fulfils a contract in a professional capacity, to be forming a company and bidding on this business on the basis of that previous experience. I do not say that if the information is equally available to others it is necessarily wrong.
26207-1-111J
May I ask the hon. member a question?
Yes.

I think the point made by the hon. member is a very important one. Does he make that last statement without qualifications, namely that this man in the course of his business-and I take it quite properly-having obtained certain information which is not confidential, is limited in his use of it? Is that what the hon. member is saying?

No. I am not saying that at all. What I am saying is this. There is apt to be a misunderstanding if a company is formed so quickly afterwards by someone who has had this kind of professional connection. I think the hon. member for Greenwood has a sense similar to my own in these matters. I would take it that he would prefer not to be associated with such a matter so soon after he had had this professional connection with the department. It is apt to give rise to the kind of thing that has arisen in this case. But what I think is certainly very dubious procedure if the letter that was read was an authentic letter, was for these gentlemen to go out and suggest that this firm could use its influence to get a contract for another company and get a percentage on it. I did not like that. I did not think that we had that sort of thing here. I have read about these people in another country. However, I did not like it at all and I did not think the hon. lady liked it either.

No. I did not like it either, regardless of whether or not it was proper business procedure. But in any event, as I said a little while ago, he would not have gotten away with it because he could not have possibly made good his offer.
With regard to the matter of surrender may I say that, after all, this is a crop that is being taken off. It is not the surrender of land as land.
I know that.

However, the details of the contract will be presented to the band and efforts will be made to ensure that they understand the implications of any future tenders which are forthcoming.
With regard to export permits may I say that I think the hon. member has sufficient knowledge of governmental affairs to know that the Department of Trade and Commerce would hardly give an export permit to an unknown person for an unknown type of material. If my information is correct I think the line is drawn with regard to timber as to the type which it is expected to export. For instance, I think there may be some difficulty
1754	HOUSE OF
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration in some places in getting permits to export fir, but with regard to some other types of lumber the acquisition of an export permit is almost automatic. Again I am not sufficiently well versed in the affairs of export permits and the department's activities in this field to make a firm statement. However, I do not think this is a field in which the department can secure for a third party a permit to export X products in X quantities. Therefore, I really cannot agree with the hon. member there.

I might point out that I do not regard the Indian affairs branch as exactly an unknown quantity. After all, the price that the minister can get-and that is what she is doing; she is acting as trustee for the Indians-for this timber is perhaps going to be dependant upon whether or not it can be exported. Therefore the minister as superintendent general and as trustee should find out from her colleague first whether or not export permits for this tract of timber in these circumstances will be available. On that fact would depend the kind of business transaction she could make. She is not like anybody else; she is not like the minister in any other department. She is a trustee in a very special sense. That is something of which I am sure she is well aware.

I am quite willing to explore the proposition which has been put forward by the hon member. However, before I leave this debate-and I presume it is over now-I may say this to the hon. member who has just taken his seat and who expressed concern about whether or not the information was available to all parties. I refer him to page 1725 of Hansard-I have now looked the matter up-and the remarks of the hon. member for Niagara Falls. I think he will find that she said that the department, in letters of May 24 and June 25, gave Beaufort the same information as that contained in the letter which was read.

May I make one inquiry of the minister. If in fact, all of this information which F. G. J. Johnson and Associates Limited obtained is readily available, can she speculate why Mr. Johnson was of the opinion that it was saleable information?
For all I know, he may have written the letter in response to an inquiry. I do not know what went on previously. I am not a mind reader. I would not indulge in speculation on this matter.
