speechtext: It being five o'clock it is my duty to leave the chair in order that the house may proceed to private members business, in pursuance of standing order 15.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: It being five o'clock the house will proceed to private members' business as listed on today's order paper, namely private bills and public bills.

The house in committee on Bill No. S-6, to incorporate Cochin Pipe Lines Ltd.-Mr. Nugent-Mr. Martineau in the chair.
On clause 1-Incorporation.

I was a member of the committee that examined those who are interested in having this bill passed. I am not rising in order to take any objection to the passage of this particular bill. I have received no specific complaints from anybody or any indication that anybody should stand in the way of its passage. However, it was brought out that the applicants for this charter were reluctant to spend even $50,000 for the purposes of getting information as to the feasibility, as it was called, of their program, despite the fact that, having regard to the proposed share capital, we have in contemplation a $4 million company.
My information is to the effect that this is the first time the committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines has been prepared to grant a charter before the applicants for the charter had taken the matter sufficiently seriously to invest a modest amount of their own money in a feasibility study of the project. I am informed that if that is to be the policy in the future, a precedent of some consequence may be established here.
The suggestion was made that now that we have a national energy board, parliamentary responsibility is practically removed. I cannot believe that is the intent of the statute or we would not be insisting that a parliamentary charter is required in connection with the pipe line business. It was also brought out that the circumstances are perhaps unusual this session. The applicants may have come to parliament without some of the advance work or preparation of feasibility studies that have been presented in the past because there may be an inclination to believe that we might not be here for very long. I think the committee was prepared to be generous, having regard to these circumstances.
Then I do point out that we have notice on the order paper today of a bill for the incorporation of another pipe line company. I believe the government should look at this

matter. They amended the pipe line legislation, and I think we should be informed soon as to whether or not it is the wish of the government that henceforth it will be possible to obtain a charter for a pipe line company without the applicants having probed very deeply into the feasibility of the project; that they should come forward with practically no personal investment prior to the application for a charter. I am told that a charter of this kind, just assuming that the present applicants do not do anything else, has a considerable commercial value. If hon. members will look at the clauses of the bill they will see that, while we are told the intention is to build a particular pipe line from town A to town B, there is nothing in the bill to restrict the applicant to the building of a pipe line over that particular route.
While I am not proposing to oppose this particular application, in large measure because of the uncertainty of the length of this session, and while I have no animosity towards the applicants-I know none of them- and no one has approached me who has an interest in another pipe line to indicate that this pipe line application should be opposed. I do believe this question should be examined by the minister concerned. He should be very careful in the future as to whether or not people, without any feasibility studies and with practically no investment except legal fees, should be able to come to a parliamentary committee and obtain a charter, thus obtaining something with the substantial value connected with a charter of this kind. We should consider carefully whether or not they should be able to obtain this charter without restriction, and convey that to persons who are not referred to in the list of applicants for incorporation.

I should like to follow up the remarks made by the previous speaker. I have been told that a charter of this type has extraordinary commercial value. I have been told further that it is most unusual to have the House of Commons and Senate asked to give powers in such a bill without any particulars as to what is to be done once the pipe line bill is passed.
I recall that on the introduction of this bill certain statements were made by the sponsor. I draw attention of hon. members to the fact, as I gather the previous speaker did, that nowhere in the clauses of this bill are we told the specific purpose for which this bill is being enacted. In the past nine years we have incorporated quite a number of pipe line companies. If my memory is correct, in all of those bills there was at least some outline
Private Bills
of what was going to be done, where the pipe line was going to function and for what purpose.
No, that is not so.

In most of them, I think you will find a specific statement of the purpose of the bill. You will find general powers, yes. I am referring particularly to the bills we have dealt with in the last two years. In this bill you will also find certain absolute powers. I know we should not refer to the clauses at the moment, but hon. members should look at the powers set forth in clause 6. This clause grants absolute powers not only for development, for operations, maintenance, control, leasing, mortgaging, hypothecating, and so on, but also powers of a provincial nature, an interprovincial nature and an international nature.
I say therefore that when we have a bill in which the particulars are not set forth, that is the building of a pipe line from town A to town B or whatever it is, we have a responsibility to ask the sponsor for the most complete information in connection with the bill. I think, too, we have a responsibility to ask the minister of the crown for his advice about passing such a generally all-powerful bill of the nature of the one before us.

I wish to give the committee a little more information. Apparently the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River, who was in the standing committee, found the evidence given was not such as to satisfy him on the feasibility of the project. With all due respect, I think that perhaps we did not give quite enough information about the people forming this company. Information was given that this will be a wholly owned subsidiary of the Bannister Construction Company Limited, which is a purely Canadian company. It is a very large company in the pipe line contracting business and has many years experience in the building of pipe lines throughout Canada, from Canada to outside countries, and so on. They have very competent engineers and economists. They are always studying this question of where and when a potential market for transporting oil or gas or petroleum products may arise, because that is the sort of thing they have to investigate in order to plan ahead for their own pipe line operations. I suggest that when these gentlemen come into the house and say that they see a potential market here, it is not quite fair to say there is no feasibility study at all and that there is an additional sum of $50,000 to $150,000 which they will have to spend after they are incorporated in order to justify what they believe now, by really examining the market and examining

Private Bills
in detail all these things with which they have some experience and about which they have some reason for believing, are very feasible.
However, this question of whether they should have done this extra detailed feasibility study is complicated by one point that I do not think was brought out too clearly here, although it was before a Senate committee. In Canada there are in existence several pipe lines which have powers about the same as this one and which, having a dominion statute, could find it necessary to go before the energy board of a province, or the national energy board where it is between two provinces, and we would find such companies perhaps being empowered to do something that had never been contemplated when we first granted the acts to incorporate them.
Not only that, in this particular field certain of these gentlemen have a very good idea of potential market that may or may not be large enough to warrant starting construction now, but which they feel is going to be large enough very soon to require a pipe line and have the capacity to support a pipe line. They feel that since this is such a natural prospect there is nothing to stop anyone else now having a pipe line from taking a look at it and jumping to the national energy board to ask for permission to do this. In order to complete their move with the national energy board they have to be incorporated and it seems to me to be good planning on their part, once they are satisfied that there is the potential and that it is worth while going after, to get into a corporate position so that they would not be behind the eight ball if anyone else took up the idea once it became public.
I suggest, in order to be fair to these gentlemen who have seen the potential and are prepared to do this, we should allow them to get their corporate status so that they would not be in an unfair position with respect to anyone else who would want to seize on their idea and beat them out of it.
As to the particulars in this bill, we have not asked for a specific power to go from Hughenden, Alberta to Melville, Saskatchewan. The feasibility study might possibly extend the line a few miles past Melville. Since this is a new and growing industry there is every possibility that in years to come there will be a necessity or a need to extend the pipe line further, and I suggest it would be unduly restrictive on the company to come in and ask for a specific line from one point to another and then, following the feasibility study, have to come back to parliament to amend the bill so that it could change that again.
[Mr. Nugent.J
I suggest that the powers conferred by this bill are not out of line. I took the trouble to check the other statutes and, having done so, I found nothing in this one that was out of line with the general powers conferred on other pipe line companies, and I do not think it is so broad a power that it would be abused. I suggest there must be a certain amount of flexibility and I suggest to hon. members of the committee, in that this is a new sort of project in a new area where there is an increasing demand for propanes, butanes, and the like, that this company does need as much flexibility as is provided, and I hope hon. members can see it that way.

Clause agreed to.
On clause 2-Provisional directors.

Members of the committee will recall that I asked counsel for the proposed company to what extent they had looked at precedents and to what extent this bill closely followed the pattern of previous pipe line bills, particularly recent pipe line bills. The hon. member for Vancouver East said that in relation to some previous bills he thought this one was open to criticism because it did not specify the route. I do not think that has been a customary practice in the incorporation of these companies.
However, if we do not have the feasibility study and if we do not have a particular route, as in the case of railroad licences, I would like to know why these companies come to parliament at all if we are simply to be a rubber stamp and take the attitude that the national energy board will look into this later. I think the minister should review the parent act to see whether we should take up our time in the House of Commons in this way when the pattern is the same as in previous bills dealing with routes "within or outside Canada" interprovincially or otherwise. I do not know why we should seek to deal with these matters whatsoever.
In connection with clause 2 I would raise this question for the committee. To what extent is it a departure from recent pipe line bills? I find a rather important one here, particularly important to those of us in the House of Commons who remember when the Conservative opposition had a great deal to say about "Canada first" in connection with pipe line activities. That was the cry right across the country in the 1957 and 1958 elections-protecting Canadians and protecting assets such as pipe lines for Canadians. They created a great horror around the country with respect to the word "export", but now this sponsor has indicated to us that the right to export is the same although we do not know over what route.

To me it seems significant that the last pipe line bill seeking incorporation of a company last session-although there may have been others and I have indicated I was not a member of the committee for some years-contained the following as clause 2, which became section 2 of the act of incorporation:
(1) The persons named in section 1 of this act shall be the first directors of the company.
I am referring to the Aurora Pipe Line Company, the act respecting which was assented to on July 13, 1961. Therefore it is one of the most recent pipe line measures passed by the house, and it has an additional subsection (2) in section 2 which reads:
All the directors of the company shall at all times be Canadian citizens ordinarily resident in Canada.
There is nothing of that kind in this bill. I had not looked at the precedents before going to the committee meeting but had relied on counsel for the company to point out to me in what way this particular bill differed in so far as some other recent parliamentary incorporations were concerned.
I just point this out to hon. members on the government side who talked so much about keeping these matters Canadian. Now they are apparently prepared to accept this form of incorporation which is in no way comparable to what was in the bill to which I refer.

On that I would first point out that these are all Canadian citizens. It is all Canadian money. It is going to be a subsidiary of Bannister Construction Company, a company which has always had all Canadian directors. Perhaps they felt it was not necessary to put that clause in, not having any other plans. I wish that had been asked of the company's solicitor in the committee. I never thought to ask it, but I am sure that is the situation. These are Edmonton residents; they are Canadians; it is a Canadian company and intends to remain that way.

There is not anybody here so naive as not to know it is possible to transfer shares from a Canadian to a nonresident. At any time it is possible for the shareholders to vote the election of directors, and regardless of what the present intention is, or regardless of the fact that at the moment the people seeking incorporation are all Canadians-I am not in any way questioning their good faith or anything like that-let us not overlook the fact that unless a clause of that kind is included there is nothing to prevent the incorporators selling their shares after the company is incorporated; there is
Private Bills
nothing to prevent the directorate of the company being composed of non-Canadians.
I am not insisting that they be Canadians, but I am pointing out that in days that I very well remember there was the hue and cry on the part of the people who form today's government that these pipe line companies were being transferred to foreigners and that we should be insisting on Canada first as I remember the slogan. I do not think in this kind of bill that principle is receiving the support necessary to protect the country in this way.

Clause agreed to.
Clauses 3 to 5 inclusive agreed to.
On clause 6-Power to construct and operate pipe lines.

With regard to clause 6, Mr. Chairman, again when I refer to the precedent of the Aurora Pipe Line Company of last year I find they asked for extraprovincial and international pipe lines, but not interprovincial pipe lines. What is the significance of asking for interprovincial pipe lines in one bill and not in another?

I think Aurora was designed to carry a line from Alberta into Montana strictly across an international boundary, whereas this pipe line is designed, in the first instance at least, to carry these products from the province of Alberta into the province of Saskatchewan. It may in the future go further, but that is why it is interprovincial at the present time.

Mr. Chairman, in connection with clause 6 (a) some legal counsel for whom I have a great deal of respect have said that this clause is much broader than had been possible in some previous pipe line bills. One of the points that was drawn to my attention was that paragraph (a) of this clause says that the rights will extend within or outside Canada to do such and such. It was pointed out to me that in some other bills it was specifically stated that the powers would be confined to certain geographical areas or to certain provinces.
Frankly, I was not very impressed with the fact that we are being unduly generous here when we do not refer to provinces, because the bill of last year to which I referred did, of course, mention some provincial boundaries. It practically took in the waterfront because it mentioned Alberta, Saskatchewan, Manitoba, British Columbia, the Northwest Territories and the Yukon. I do not think this is particularly significant; I think the main thing is whether or not we are going to

Pension Act
grant these charters automatically without having very much information presented to us concerning the feasibility of these projects.
Clause 6 agreed to.
Clauses 7 to 11 inclusive agreed to.

Preamble agreed to.
Title agreed to.
Bill reported, read the third time passed.

subtopic: AMENDMENT PROVIDING FOR APPEAL TO COURTS

speakeroldname: Mr. Jack McIntosh (Swift Current-Maple Creek) moved
subtopic: AMENDMENT PROVIDING FOR APPEAL TO COURTS
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. C-21 to amend the Pension Act (judicial appeal).
He said: Mr. Speaker, my charge by the introduction of a private members' bill, now numbered C-21, is that the present members of the pension commission are not carrying out the intent of parliament and that the Pension Act as now constituted is, I believe, contrary to the Canadian Bill of Rights.
The purpose of the bill, as set out in the explanatory notes, is to give an applicant for a pension under the Pension Act the right, where the pension commission or an appeal board has ruled against his or her entitlement, to have the decision reviewed by the courts, first on any question of law respecting the interpretation of the
[Mr. Benidickson.l
Pension Act, and second on those controversial issues of fact which must be weighed, as the courts are used to doing, in the knowledge of human conduct and intention. An ancillary purpose gives the commission itself the right to refer any question of law to the Supreme Court of Canada.
The bill applies to the Pension Act that principle of the rule of law that, to the degree and most possible, the decisions of an administrative tribunal or commission which touch the person, property or rights of an individual should be subject to review by the courts.
The United Kingdom has applied this rule of law to as many of its boards, tribunals and commissions as possible in the tribunals and inquiries act, 1958. The British parliament found it was necessary to protect the rights of the individual by guaranteeing an appeal to the courts from arbitrary tribunal decisions. I would submit that a study of only a few decisions handed down by our present pension commission would convince the people of Canada that this branch of the department is in the hands of bureaucrats who circumvent the law because of their powers under section 65(3) of the Pension Act. Section 65(3) of this act states:
Except as hereinafter otherwise provided every decision of an appeal board of the commission is final.
I submit that this section of the Pension Act conflicts with and is contradictory to the intention of the Canadian Bill of Rights, which to me means that every individual in Canada is entitled to the protection of the courts.
The introduction of this bill probably would not be necessary if I felt that the present members of the pension commission were capable or qualified to perform the duties expected of them by the past and present members of this house. It would seem that the present commission feels that it has the right, under the present Pension Act, to substitute the commissioner's views for the views of parliament.
It is obvious that the basic purpose of the statute is to protect service personnel against the risks to which by reason of their service they were, or are, exposed. There are two main principles which I believe the people of Canada through their members of parliament expected the commission to keep before them; first, that of basic fairness to the taxpayers of Canada, and second, justice to those who have served and are now serving in our forces.
I charge that the commission is not adhering to either of these principles and I would be quite prepared to prove my point in a court of law with evidence presently in my possession. A study of the speeches of

ministers and members of parliament responsible for the implementation of this act would confirm that the pension commission in the interpretation of the various provisions of the act should do so with a view to extending the broadest and most liberal application, consistent with the intention and terms of the statute. In fact, such words have been uttered by our present Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Churchill) as well as by others who held that portfolio before him.
I am sure the people of Canada feel there can be little argument against the nation's providing compensation to a man or his dependants for any disability or death which arises out of, or is caused by, the performance of his duties.
In order to give direction to the commission as to the intent of parliament, section 70 of the act was inserted in 1948. It is commonly called by veterans the benefit of doubt section, and reads as follows:
Notwithstanding anything in this act, on any application for pension, the applicant is entitled to the benefit of the doubt, which means that it is not necessary for him to adduce conclusive proof of his right to the pension applied for, but the body adjudicating on the claim shall draw from all the circumstances of the case, the evidence adduced and medical opinions, all reasonable inferences and presumptions in favour of the applicant.
Ordinarily, one would assume that such a clause in the act could not be misinterpreted. It is very clear and broad and, as parliament intended, gives the administrative machinery the power to adjudicate claims with all the justice and fairness to which our service personnel are entitled. However the real test of any legislation is in its administration. In many instances the results of the administration under the present pension commission are a mockery of justice and an insult to the present and past members of this house who were charged with formulating the present Pension Act.
The effect of the present legislation has been to establish a tribunal so powerful that its members are a law unto themselves in regard to any application for pension from members of our armed forces. In this branch of the department, as in others, it is government by commission, not by the elected representatives of the people. It would appear the members of this tribunal are not concerned with the thoughts or intent of the members who drew up this act, otherwise they would have reviewed the committee minutes and Hansard when this act was passed and amended. The intended broadness of interpretation was expressed on those occasions by many speakers, including the ministers in charge of the department.
It would also appear that the members of the pension commission pay no attention to 26207-1-112
Pension Act
other aids under our statutes which would assist them with interpretation if there was any doubt in their minds. I refer now to section 15 of the Interpretation Act which applies to all our laws, with the exception of the criminal law, and which states:
Every act, and every piovision and enactment thereof, shall be deemed remedial whether its immediate purport is to direct the doing of anything that parliament deems to be for the public good, or to prevent or punish the doing of anything that seems contrary to the public good; and shall accordingly receive such fair, large and liberal construction and interpretation as will best ensure the attainment of the object of the act and of such provision or enactment, according to its true intent meaning and spirit.
This section of the Interpretation Act was inserted on the basis that the law as it existed perhaps did not do justice to some person, or group of persons. Therefore parliament gives the person or persons affected a right and a remedy.
A judge, I am informed, looks for the person whom the law was intended to benefit. In connection with the Pension Act, it would be a veteran or a veteran's dependants. In applying the law he gives the right and the remedy to these persons. A court gives to the words used by parliament a large, fair and liberal construction so as best to ensure the object of the act which, in the case of the Pension Act, is to give the veterans and their dependants rights and remedies which they did not have before the act was passed-in other words, justice.
The Pension Act as amended is a remedial statute. To illustrate how small and narrow the thinking of some of the members on the pension commission can be, I would refer hon. members to the evidence of the vicechairman of the Canadian pension commission, as recorded on May 18, 1961, in the minutes of proceedings on veterans affairs. Referring to one case, the reason for the decision was as follows:
He went across the street and delivered the message, stepped out of the door and was hit by a truck. If he had been hit going in the door, before he had delivered the message, he would have been pensionable; however, he was hit when he went out the door, and he was not pensionable.
In a communication from the chairman of the pension commission, I am informed that the commission in making its decisions is governed by certain guiding principles largely based on precedent. If the statement of the vice-chairman to the veterans affairs committee regarding the individual who was hit by a truck after he came out of the door is an example of a precedent used by the commission in establishing a ruling for other cases, we can understand why there is such widespread dissatisfaction with this method of adjudication, because the reason for the

Pension Act
decision is ridiculous and asinine; it could only be dreamed up by very narrow-minded persons.
I further charge there is no consistency in the reasons for the decisions handed down by this board of bureaucrats. I refer once again to the additional remarks of the vicechairman of the commission as recorded in the minutes I made reference to a few moments ago. As reported at the bottom of page 281, he states in part:
However, if on the other hand he was warned to go on mess parade and then slips on the steps of the mess hall, since a mess parade is not obligatory .. . that is not a valid reason and if he was hurt, he would not be pensionable.
There are many cases on file where the decisions of the board are absolutely contrary to the information given to the members of the veterans affairs committee by the vicechairman of the commission. I have the records of one case dated June 20, 1955, which in part state as follows:
On leaving the mess hall, he tripped on a small obstruction on the landing in front of the mess hall door and fell down the exterior mess hall steps. The board found that the evidence established that the accident was sustained during service in the course of carrying out his duties and that the injury must be considered to have arisen out of, and to have been directly connected with, his service, within the meaning of section 13 (2).
Either this decision was wrong or the information given to the committee by the vicechairman was wrong. The two statements are in direct contradiction to one another.
Bill No. C-21 is a bill to amend the Pension Act to provide the veteran and the serviceman and their dependants with an appeal to the courts from a decision of the pension commissioners on points of the interpretation of law. The bill also provides that the power given the board to define its own constituting act shall be subject to review by the Supreme Court of Canada. In my opinion, a commission is the poorest judge of its own measure and particularly in this case where the members of the board have no specialized knowledge. There is a principle of British law that every member of the public has a right of access to the courts to determine his rights under the law. Let us see that our service personnel are granted this same privilege.
I am aware, I may say at this point, that the Royal Canadian Legion has, on occasion, not agreed with what I am saying today and that at its Edmonton convention held two years ago the Legion asked the dominion executive council to bring in a report on the desirability of establishing an appeal from the pension commission to an independent authority. The veterans welfare advisory committee decided that such a vote was not desirable for the reason-and I quote in part-

that "The present legislation and procedure is basically sound". I suggest it is not basically sound, because it is contrary to the British theory of constitutional law which states that the subject always has a right of appeal to an independent judiciary body. Section 5 (5) of the Pension Act reads as follows:
The commission shall determine any question of interpretation of this act and the decision of the commission on any such question is final.
The question I would ask at this point is: how is the executive of the Royal Canadian Legion going to force members of the pension commission to interpret the Pension Act in a basically sound manner, or in the way parliament intended in the first place?
The executive of the Legion in another part of their report make this statement:
The pension commission interprets the benefit of doubt clause to mean that the veteran must create the doubt.
Surely the Canadian Legion does not agree with such an interpretation. In fact, a reference to their objection on this very point is made in each of their briefs dealing with section 70 of the Pension Act. I have three briefs here and in each they disagree with this interpretation of section 70 by the commission. Time does not permit me to place on the record extracts from the briefs.
I direct the attention of hon. members to words spoken by the present Prime Minister when he was the private hon. member for Prince Albert as reported at page 5895 of Hansard of July 12, 1956:
-I believe that in such a case as this consideration should be given to the amendment of the Pension Act so far as interpretation of the law is concerned so that recourse to the courts will be available to any aggrieved person to ascertain in the courts whether or not that person comes within the ambit of the legal definitions provided in the Pension Act.
May I conclude my remarks on this measure by quoting a portion of a letter I have received:
Our Canadian veterans and servicemen preferred, and still prefer, to die on their feet. Dead-their widows and fatherless children are required to live on their knees before the officials of the Canadian pension appeal board.
I solicit the support of all hon. members of the house and particularly veterans in the passing of this bill.

subtopic: AMENDMENT PROVIDING FOR APPEAL TO COURTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is a rather lengthy bill considering that it is a private member's bill. While we may not agree with all the details set forth in it nevertheless I believe the general principle of the bill is sound and because at this stage we are concerned only with the principle I should like to indicate my support for the measure.

I cannot, however, go along with the sponsor of the bill in his remarks about the pension board. I feel we should debate this bill on its merits and not on the merits of the personnel comprising the board or their competence to administer this legislation.
I support the bill because I believe it is basically sound that every person should have the right to appeal to a court of justice if he has a grievance. Without that, as the hon. member said, we have government by commission.
My own experience with the pension board has been somewhat different from that outlined by the hon. member. Hon. gentlemen know there is one matter about which I have complained over and over again. But by and large my experience with the pension board is that they have gone all out wherever possible to give favourable consideration and to extend the benefit of doubt in cases I have brought to their attention. I think that is even more true of the present board than it has been in the past.
However, I feel we must all agree that there is difficulty when a body confines itself to the interpretation of just one set of laws. There is a tendency to become routine and mechanical in the judgment of different cases and to overlook the relationship between the law that body is administering and the greater body of law which might be related to it. The sponsor of the bill mentioned the relationship of the veterans charter to the Interpretation Act. That is certainly one consideration; but there are others. I feel there is a general spirit which pervades all the laws included in the veterans charter and that general spirit, I think, reflects the spirit of parliament itself. When there is a conflict between the letter and the spirit of any particular law I think that should be subjugated to the overriding spirit of the legislation as a whole.
Apart from that there is the overriding spirit of the British North America Act which is our constitution and certainly all our laws should be interpreted within that framework. The one exception to which I referred a while ago, a question which I have frequently raised in this house, is in relation to the interpretation that has been placed on veterans legislation with regard to Newfoundland veterans. The terms of union are part of the British North America Act and therefore part of our constitution. I feel that any interpretation of veterans legislation should be interpreted in the light of our constitution.
I believe the present legislation, worded as it is, is cast in language sufficiently broad to include Newfoundland veterans under the veterans charter, but the pension commission that existed at the time of confederation when 26207-1-112J
Pension Act
this problem first arose chose to interpret it in a very different manner. Regardless of the fact that the definition of a veteran under the War Veterans Allowance Act, the Veterans Rehabilitation Act and the War Service Grants Act is broad enough to include a Newfoundland veteran the wording is not clear in the Pension Act. Although it could be interpreted as being broad enough to include Newfoundland veterans the pension commission chose not to interpret it as being sufficiently broad. Consequently Newfoundland veterans are treated as Canadians who served in the imperial forces rather than as Canadians who served in the Canadian forces.
I use that example to illustrate the point brought out by the sponsor of the bill that there is need for an independent authority to examine decisions from time to time. It is only human to make wrong judgments. Certainly every Canadian, especially now that we have a bill of rights should have an opportunity of taking his grievance before a court of law.
I do not intend to speak at length. Time is passing quickly and I know other hon. members wish to express their views. I support the general principle of the bill because I feel it is in line with the bill of rights and provides an additional safeguard for the veterans. It is one more step toward ensuring the welfare of our veterans. The principle of the bill is in line with the spirit of legislation we have already passed.
With respect to the charges that have been laid against the personnel of the pension commission I presume the minister will have something to say on their behalf.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I read this most interesting bill very carefully. I appreciate the hon. member's concern for the welfare of veterans and their dependants. I know his motives are lily white. It is evident the hon. member has given considerable thought to the problem and has spent considerable time in the preparation of the measure now before the house. The vigour of his remarks is further evidence of his deep concern for the matter and his quite unusual attack on the personnel of the Canadian pension commission is evidence of his strong feelings in the matter.
I might say that the principle and purpose of this bill have been discussed over a great number of years by veterans organizations and other people concerned with the welfare of the veterans and their dependants. The very same principle and purpose have also been discussed by trade unions all across Canada in reference to various workmen's compensation acts. It is natural for the subject

Pension Act
repeatedly to arise and for persons to consider that there should be an appeal to the courts against a decision of the commission and of what the hon. member would term- and I can well understand his point of view- established bureaucracies. However, the veterans organizations throughout the years have studied this question.
I have had some experience with the Canadian Pension Act since 1939 as an active officer of the Royal Canadian Legion, as a member of this house and as a member of the veterans affairs committee. I have listened carefully to these arguments because they merit careful consideration whether they are in support of the principle for amendment to the Pension Act or to the various workmen's compensation acts across Canada. However, in every case to date the discussion has ended, as the hon. member has pointed out, in the organizations in question-and I also mention the labour organizations-rejecting the principle and purpose of the bill as not being in the best interests of the pensioner and dependants or, shall I say, of the person on compensation. They considered-and I am just repeating their views-that there was a greater hazard to these persons directly concerned in providing for an appeal to the courts than there was in improving the legislation. I must say this. While on occasions I have differed with the Canadian pension commission in their decisions, as I am sure have many others in this house, we must remember that the Canadian pension commission is a group of citizens who are all veterans, and who have been given the responsibility of administering the Canadian Pension Act. Without doubt, from our point of view, they err on occasions.
However, I was rather surprised to hear the usually genial and mellow member's caustic comments on this occasion. As I said, the commission members are all veterans and I am sure they have at heart the welfare of veterans. The chairman, as a matter of fact, is an appointee of the present government. I think he has rendered good service as chairman of the commission, as have other members of the commission throughout the years. We must remember that the decisions of the commission are in the main based on medical evidence and on hearings that are held and the various procedures under the Canadian Pension Act to which effect is given. As I said before, while on occasion without doubt we differ with them in their decisions, the members of the commission have no reason whatever to deny an applicant a pension on any personal ground. It is human to err. They are required to make their decisions on the

basis of the evidence before them, and I am quite confident that they make their decisions according to their best judgment.
In my opinion, the remedy for the situation is this. I quite realize that improvements can be made in the Canadian Pension Act. In my opinion and, I believe, in that of the members whom I have the honour to represent in this distinguished corner of the house, the remedy is to amend the Canadian Pension Act so as to clarify certain sections and, in so doing, to remove a certain measure of ambiguity that exists at the present time, thereby strengthening the hands of the Canadian pension commission.
I think the hon. member has rendered a service by bringing to the attention of the house a bill highlighting this problem. I trust his bringing this matter to the attention of the house will cause the government to pay particular attention to the problem presented at this time and to bring in amendments that will clarify the Canadian Pension Act and thus will make the work of the Canadian pension commission less subject to criticism and easier for its members.
In addition to that, Mr. Speaker, I strongly suggest that the hon. member send copies of his bill and copies of today's Hansard to the dominion officers of the various veterans organizations across Canada and that he also ask them to make recommendations with respect to amendments to the Canadian Pension Act in order to achieve the objective which I am sure is the desire of the hon. member who introduced the bill and of all other hon. members in this house.

The hour for the consideration of private business having expired, the house will revert to the business which was interrupted at five o'clock.

The house in committee of supply, Mr. Martineau in the chair.

Indian affairs branch-Indian agencies-
618. Operation and maintenance-further amount required. $136,000.
At six o'clock the committee took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The committee resumed at 8 p.m.

When we were about to rise at five o'clock, Mr. Chairman, I asked that this particular item be not voted on at that time. I did so, sir, because-and I hope you will

agree with me-I hate to disagree with the minister in certain statements she has made about whether or not we are in order on one aspect of the matters now being discussed. I would draw your attention to the fact we are now discussing vote 618 of the supplementary estimates. This vote is for $136,000 for Indian agencies, operation and maintenance.
If I could put it briefly, Mr. Chairman, it has always been my understanding that when a supplementary estimate deals with operation and maintenance of Indian agencies, we can then raise matters of policy upon which we would like to have information. On that understanding, therefore, that I am speaking only because of vote 618, there is a question which I should like to direct to the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration in her capacity as the minister in charge of Indian affairs. I do so, Mr. Chairman, because it is of the utmost importance in every way that there should be established the finest possible relationship between the government in the operation of the Indian agencies and the Indian agencies in their relationships with our first Canadian citizens, whether they be on reservations or under treaty.
I would, therefore, under this supplementary vote like to ask the minister if she is in a position to give the committee any information relative to the most extraordinary letter that I believe was sent to all members of the House of Commons under date of February 23, 1962, from the Indian defense league of America. In this letter there are some remarkable statements made of a nature which I believe should be clarified and answered as soon as possible in order to maintain the best possible relationship between the government department, the Indian agencies in all the provinces and our first native Canadian citizens. May I, Mr. Chairman, just take a moment to quote from this letter:
With due respect for the parliament of Canada, we express our opinion to the honourable members, concerning Indian affairs which was consistently evaded in the past by the administration. It is with sincere regret that I draw the attention of the house assembled, the fact that our allIndian organization was not given the courtesy of appearing before the joint committee of the House of Commons and the Canadian Senate dealing with Indian affairs, thus ignoring our request. We were of the opinion that the august body was to receive representations from Indians organizations with the opportunity of supporting their briefs with oral testimony, supported by official record.
This is the introduction. As a matter of fact, as I went through this letter, sir, I was not quite certain as to whether or not the Six Nations assembly was declaring war on Canada. However, they do say this in the second paragraph of the letter, and this is important because, if my knowledge of history is correct, the Six Nations is a most
13,	1962	1763
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration important body in Canada and many years ago was important to Canada in fighting on behalf of Her Majesty at that time:
We are aghast at the attitude of the department of Indian affairs. We have been shocked at the evasive replies on questions sent to the department concerning the obligation of protection of the Six Nations under unabrogated treaties with Great Britain.
I know, without going any farther, that the minister will understand why I raise this question. I am certain, Mr. Chairman, that the minister and the members of the committee realize I am taking this course because this kind of letter sent to members of parliament by our native Indians on a matter of this nature, added to the matter on which we spent four hours previously, should be answered as quickly as possible. I hope that under this supplementary vote which deals with Indian agencies, the minister will feel this is the occasion to make a real statement of government policy concerning the attitude of her department to Indian affairs and to answer such charges as these. This letter is sent over the name of the Indian defense league of America, in the name of the Six Nations confederacy, to all members of parliament. If the information is incorrect, then let the minister get up and explain in what way it is incorrect. If there is any way of bringing about a greater understanding, a better relationship, if she has some new policy in mind, surely this is the time to make a statement and not wait until the general estimates are before the committee.
First of all, I should like to ask the hon. member, since he did not mention it, from what domicile is that letter? Where did it come from?

This is from the Indian defense league of America, home office, box 305, Niagara Falls, New York. According to this, it represents the Six Nations confederacy in the United States and Canada, and includes a letter sent to the hon. members of the joint committee of the House of Commons and Senate of Canada, on behalf of the confederacy.

I think the answer is simple. We appointed the committee and, as the hon. member knows, the committee undertook to hear representatives from the various Indian groups. I do not know of the Indian defence league, though I recognize the name of Mr. Antone. I have seen his name on letters from time to time. He is domiciled in the state of New York and it is true that the Six Nations Indians are on both sides of the border. If my memory serves me well the Caughnawagas did not make any representations, although they were invited to
1764	HOUSE OF
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration do so and they are a member of the confederation, but the Six Nations Indians at Brantford made two representations. One was made by the hereditary chiefs organization and the other by the elected council organization; so I think in so far as the Six Nations Indians within Canada are concerned, they were heard.
I do not know if that answers the hon. member's question or not, but further than that I would have to refer to the committee itself as offhand I do not recall all who were heard by the committee. However it is certain that an invitation would not go outside Canada to an organization which is an international organization.

I am somewhat familiar with this confederation as I have the honour to be an adopted daughter of the Mohawks of the Six Nations. I have some knowledge of this particular group since I addressed a meeting of them not too long ago. As the minister said, they are an international organization and they are particularly concerned with some treaties. I had also the honour to be a member of the joint committee for the past year, but not for the first two years.
At its meetings I raised some questions the answers to which rather stunned me, and perhaps the minister can tell me why such answers were given. I had been asked by the Indian defence league to inquire if there was a copy in existence of the treaties signed by John Graves Simcoe. I was informed that the branch did not have copies of these treaties. I inquired if a search had ever been made among the imperial records because they seemed to be so basic to the Indians' view of their rights. As I recall it the director said no research had been made among the imperial records for the originals of these treaties, and since they are so basic to what the Indians believe are their rights I wonder if the minister can advise us why this has not been done.
There is one thing with reference to the matter which we were discussing here this afternoon which my hon. friend from Vancouver mentioned earlier. That is the imputation that some individuals who represented my party were concerned in the matter. I may say that nothing could be further from the truth. Perhaps he and the minister may not know that one of the individuals who acted as agent for the Beaufort firm in Ottawa is a man from British Columbia whose name is Dean Finlayson, which name may mean more to him than to me.

There are a number of questions I should like to put to the minister relating to Indian agencies and the Indians in my area, and I may say that the impetus to


raise them at this time comes from several different sources. The minister will remember my asking her a question regarding some criticism made by Chief Crawford Adams, when several weeks ago he was quoted as saying that of the Indians in Canada those in the worst condition that he knows of are in the area north of Port Arthur.
Recently the gentleman from the other place who was honoured in being placed there by the Prime Minister because of his Indian blood, has been in a sense preaching to me, referring to the fact that it is very important I take a much keener interest in the Indians in my constituency because he feels that they are in a very poor and relatively unfortunate condition compared with most of the other Indians in this country. These are two things that have aroused my concern.
I might point out to hon. members who wonder why my interest might not have been higher, that there are somewhere between 3,000 and 5,000 Indians in my constituency. No one is quite sure about the number, and of the 2,500 estimated to have a vote in the coming election approximately 2,000 of them exist well north of the farthest railway line that bisects the constituency. Of these the largest group could only be reached by plane on a chartered flight of 385 or 390 miles from Port Arthur, which is beyond my finances, and the other large group could only be reached by flying in from Val d'Or to Winisk near Hudson's bay. Therefore my interest in most of those constituents, because they are spread out and it would be very costly to reach them, in a sense has to be from an office approach point of view. I would like to ask the minister to give me an analysis of what is being done for these Indians who are north of the C.N.R. tracks, especially Indians up from Lansdowne House, the Trout lake area and the Winisk area.
More specifically I want to deal with the whole question of elections. Hon. members will remember that recently in the Kenora by-election there was a considerable stirring up of candidates in the area over the Indian vote in that constituency and the Conservative candidate. This is something which I have brought up before with a certain amount of humour because I think the classic example was Lansdowne House. A few years ago in a provincial vote something like 130 votes went to the Conservatives, five to the Liberals, two to the communists and none to the C.C.F. candidate, and there were no spoiled ballots in this poll. It was agreed that only one or two of the people there could read or write. That is why I say it has a humourous connotation.

There is one poll in my constituency that even in his heyday the late C. D. Howe never won. It is a place called Ombabika. It is mostly Indians who vote there and we discovered that in the Lansdowne House case the white man who happened to have the most influence with the Indians was a Tory. As I say, the situation was random and humorous but I am wondering if this is going to be so in the next election because there will be so many more voters. I would like to know from the minister what plans she may have for instructing the Indians, to see that some program is carried on with these Indians in the north who really could not be reached by candidates, and to see whether some kind of fairer arrangement could be made in the future. I know hon. members will say, "Surely it is up to the party to put up scrutineers". I wonder how many political parties in Canada in a constituency association could afford to send scrutineers to polls that are 300 or 400 miles away from the centre of the riding. I wonder how many of them could afford the charter costs.
I understand that in Nova Scotia or Newfoundland very recently this challenge was put to the premier of Nova Scotia by the leader of the Conservative party, and the premier answered that he would rent an aeroplane to send them in-it was in connection with a by-election-and if the Conservatives could not afford to pay their share of the flight he would see that the Liberals picked up the charge for getting the-
What province was that?
This is in Newfoundland. There was a by-election going on, I believe, up in Labrador and evidently this became-
The hon. member understands that the Indians in Newfoundland do not come under this department, does he not? This was included in the terms of confederation.
I understood they were all killed off in Newfoundland centuries ago.

The point I am really making here is that even in Newfoundland the Conservatives find it very expensive to get scrutineers up to the Indians. I am wondering whether the minister and her officials have considered this whole question of the Indian vote in remote places and what steps can be taken to see that it is done efficiently and fairly and in the interests of all candidates.
The other point I want to raise with the minister is this. I raised it with her, she will remember, by letter. It is regarding the possibilities of Indians working on the pulp
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration and paper operations in our region. The minister will remember that I sent her some criticisms and suggestions that were expressed by the lumber and saw mill workers union, which happens to have the contracts in most of the woods industry from the Manitoba border through to north of Sudbury. The minister's reply was to the effect that these suggestions and criticisms were going to be considered immediately. I appreciate this, but I would like to know from the minister just what steps have been taken in northwestern Ontario in recent years to give the Indians some kind of permanent work or a more permanent relationship than they have at the present time.
I am sure that hon. members will have noted not too long ago that a little girl of six or seven years of age was torn to death by dogs up in a small village in my constituency, at Auden. It so happens that the dogs which tore her to death, which trapped her after her father left her outside a Sunday school, were kept by Indians who lived not too far away from Auden. The situation of these Indians near Auden, in Ombabika, is a wonderful case in point of the failure of the pulp and paper industry in the woods to find a real place for these people and to fit them in or tie them in with some kind of economic basis.
Auden is a permanent camp of the Abitibi Power and Paper Company. It has been in operation for at least seven or eight years to my knowledge. Continuous attempts have been made by the company to use Indians wherever practical but only, as I understand it-and my information is from both the union and people who you might say are on the management side-with very limited success.
I wanted to use this as an example and compare it with the situation at Longlac, which is not too far away, where the use of Indians from the Longlac reserve has been more successful on the part of the Kimberly-Clark Corporation. I would like some kind of elaboration from the minister as to the steps that have been taken of a persistent kind-at least, I hope they have been persistent-to see if some kind of continuing relationship cannot be worked out with these paper companies and with the unions for the benefit of the Indians.
The union people-I must be frank-are very critical of the Indian service, perhaps more critical than the service deserves; but I can assure the minister that their idealism in this situation is of a very substantial kind. They would be willing to go out of their way to see that the Indians were given an opportunity to have regular work whatever the relationship of the Indian might be to the
1766	HOUSE OF
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration standard kind of seniority that happens to exist and is becoming more important in the woods and forests.
The last point I should like to raise with the minister stems from a letter I have received from the Indian chief at Mobert, Ontario, which is not too far from White River. The complaints I have received from the chief really deal with the ineffectiveness of welfare provisions during the winter. He has expressed concern to me over the fact that when an Indian is sick it is almost impossible to get him out to hospitalization because no one has any money and no emergency funds are available, and he has not, according to his letter, the authority to do anything about it.
His other complaint is that assistance is not forthcoming as easily as it should be to young men of the band who do not happen to be married. He feels that there is a calculated toughness on the part of the department with these young unmarried Indians, he thinks they are being treated far too harshly and the suggestion in correspondence to me is that this should be changed.
These are some of the problems of the Indians that I thought I should bring to the minister's attention. In terms of their importance, of course, I think an attempt to work out a relationship between the woods industry, the unions engaged in that industry and the Indian affairs branch to give the Indians a steadier basis of employment in the whole region from Sioux Lookout eastward to Hornepayne, and all the way down along the lake Superior periphery, would be most advantageous.
The question of the elections is something that we can all either get worked up or irate about, or we can even see it as something very funny, but I think most hon. members of the house will realize that in the next election we are trying an experiment, in the way that this is the first time in a national sense that Indians will have had the vote. I think all of us, no matter how we might like the votes of Indians to come to our particular party, will hope that the whole matter will run off very fairly. Given the situation that we have had in northwestern Ontario in the provincial elections, there are possibilities of our doubting this situation.
The final matter is really a general one and I should just like to repeat it. I would like some estimate from the minister as to the situation of the Indians whom Chief Telford Adams has said are in the worst condition of any Indians that he knows about in Canada, and whom the Indian gentleman in the other place has suggested to me need much more looking after than they are getting at the present time.

First of all, let me say that I did answer the hon. member's letters to me and I outlined to him the situation as far as I could discover it with reference to this section of the country. I told him at that time that although Chief Telford Adams had made these statements not only this year but last year in a general way, up to the present time we had nothing to substantiate those charges. There were only his statements which we had read in the papers. We received no protest from him by way of a letter, neither did we receive any protests from people from other parts of the country so we were somewhat at a loss to know how to proceed in the absence of anything more specific.
The people to whom the hon. member refers, are largely nomads. It is hard to find them in a given place at a given time and this complicates immeasurably the problem of their care and welfare. I must say I was interested to hear about the results of previous elections. It only goes to show that one does not have to be able to read and write in order to be intelligent. I may say, though, with respect to the taking of the vote, that no matter whether it is in an urban area or a rural area or even in a remote region of Canada, that is the responsibility of the chief electoral officer, and I am sure the worst thing I could do as a minister would be to interfere in any way with voting in an election, or attempt to influence the Indians in any way whatsoever.

I did not suggest the minister should interfere but I should like to know what instructions, if any, are going out to her Indian agents with regard to this matter. I do not want to make charges in this committee in relation to this subject, but perhaps the minister will understand an assurance from me that I am certain I can explain to her why the vote is swung so strongly in some areas of the country. It has a direct relationship, in provincial elections, with the Indian agents. I should like to know what instructions are likely to be given out, and whether the agents are to be asked to go out of their way to see that in any places where they have any kind of advisory jurisdiction these things are run fairly. That is all.
No instructions go out from my department, nor will any instructions go from my department with reference to Indians in relation to elections.

Something was said a little while ago by the hon. member for Vancouver East about appearances before the joint committee. I was a member of that committee for the three years during which it functioned.

We sat through many long and weary hours over that period and I am glad to say there was very little evidence of political bias or partisanship, though possibly it did creep in in the last year. However, with regard to the right of various groups and organizations to appear I should like to refer the hon. member and others in this committee to the preamble to the second and final report of the joint committee which was filed by the chairman last year. I am reading from the second paragraph which states:
During the present session your committee completed its examination of Indian administration and thoroughly reviewed the Indian Act. Thirty five additional witnesses were heard this session. Since June, 1959, there have been 97 meetings and over 100 witnesses have been heard. In addition, included in the minutes of proceedings and evidence, as appendices thereto, are 80 written submissions received by your committee from Indian organizations and bands, provincial governments, church authorities and other organizations and groups interested in the welfare and advancement of the Indian Canadian.
My recollection is that a number of witnesses made not only one but two appearances. I had the honour to serve as vice-chairman of the committee last year and I presided at a number of meetings. We did decide at a meeting of a subcommittee on agenda and procedure to adopt the rule that where there had been one appearance there would not be another during the current year because we felt the time had come when a report should be written. With regard to the group mentioned by the hon. member, there was a discussion and in view of the fact that this particular group apparently had its headquarters outside this country, and because, as the minister has pointed out, the things they wished to say had largely been covered by previous briefs and submissions made by other groups during the course of our proceedings, we felt that no good purpose would be served by calling these people here to give evidence. Apart from that, every opportunity was given to every organization and group to make oral representations and, if they wished, to supplement them by written briefs. Those are the facts.

I should like to ask the minister a question in connection with vote 618. I noted the statement made by the hon. lady yesterday in relation to economic development. That comes under vote 622. However, I should like to ask this question under vote 618.
I have taken a keen interest in Indian affairs for around 30 years. However, I do not maintain that I am a specialist on Indian affairs, so when I learned that this vote was likely to be discussed today I looked for additional advice and information. I had a talk
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration with an hon. member in the other place. Naturally, that was Senator Gladstone who certainly must be regarded as an expert on Indian affairs. He told me that the native Indians do not want charity; they do not want to be a charge on the people of Canada. They want to be first class Canadian citizens. They want policies promulgated and put into action which will result in their being first class citizens whether on the reserves or elsewhere. One of the matters about which the hon. senator was good enough to advise me concerned the care of Indians in special circumstances-the word "charity" is not one I wish to use in this connection. I should like to link this subject with the statement made by the minister on economic development, but I shall have to deal with that subject under another vote. In view of the opinions expressed by Senator Gladstone, may I ask the minister to explain the basis upon which aid is given through the Indian agencies on these grounds of requirement and necessity? Does it differ in various parts of Canada or is there any general and basic policy? I would appreciate receiving that information. I shall leave the other aspects until we reach vote No. 622.
Do I understand that the hon. member is now asking about welfare?
Yes.

Mr. Chairman, the amounts as set out in votes Nos. 620 and 621 total $482,500 representing additional amounts required this year for welfare. Of this amount the sum of $21,000-but possibly I had better start with British Columbia and the Yukon-
I am sorry to interrupt the minister but I am not interested in the amounts. I wish to know the policy governing the granting of welfare.

Generally speaking it is on the same basis as that adopted by the various municipalities. That is to say that although in most cases the Indian bands are not treated as municipalities we do have some Indian bands that are treated as municipalities. As I say, however, by and large they are not treated as municipalities. The welfare which is handled for them is handled pretty much on the same basis as that handled in municipalities in the various provinces. In some cases the bands themselves have advanced to the stage where their own band council handles the disposition of welfare within its band. This again varies all the way from the recommendations coming from the band council and the welfare being dispensed by the superintendent, right up to
1768	HOUSE OF
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration the whole oi the revenue funds being in the hands of the band as they would be in any municipality and the band making its own budget and dispensing its own welfare to its own members, much as a municipal council would do in any municipality in Canada. That is a broad general description of the process followed. As far as education is concerned, I omitted to say previously that I was concerned about truancy, particularly with respect to children whose parents earn their livelihood by fishing and trapping beyond the municipal boundaries. What co-operation is the minister getting from the province of Ontario in enforcing the truancy laws?
The minister did not reply to my observations in respect to the United States charitable institution. I would be satisfied if she would say she would have another look at this matter.
Then I referred to one of three or four reports of sociologists and anthropologists who have gone to this area because it stands out like a sore thumb. I referred to the observations and report of the Rev. Jay, a United Church student pastor who thoughtfully wrote a report on the situation there. He said a community of this kind needed, during the bridge period, as I call it, a representative of the federal department who would be a guidance officer for these people. Is it possible to provide such a service? The author definitely advocates, in addition, a hostel for the use of people who are in transit between a reserve and a civilized community.
Kenora, through the Presbyterian church, has a new institution of whose existence I am sure the minister is aware. I hope the hon. lady will regard it very carefully. As I understand the position, no contribution has been made to this hostel by the federal government. I think that probably a contribution should be made. I believe the church on its own has paid some $30,000 initially as part of a home missionary effort to acquire the property to provide for the needs of Indians in transit in and out of Kenora, some guidance, some comfort and some amenities, even basic amenities which are not provided on the main street of the town. This kind of thing, I think, should perhaps be encouraged to some extent by the department, knowing as we do that economic opportunities are not very good for this exploding population in the north. I would hope the minister would provide to some of these communities or to the churches aid for hostels. Hostels were high on the list in the report to which I referred.

Mr. Chairman, I was under the impression that I had answered the hon. member but possibly I did not make myself clear with respect to the Amish school. I intended to include it in my reference to the

Supply-Citizenship and Immigration whole matter being under consideration. I meant the whole matter of Red Lake, including the school, too.
We are very much interested in the hostel at Kenora. I think it is an excellent step in the right direction. Personally I am not too sure that this is a matter in which Indian affairs should participate. I would think there might be a better case made for participation by the citizenship department. However, this is again a matter which is being considered. We are watching it very closely. We think it is an excellent idea. Of course, the ultimate good will come when these people are accepted into normal accommodation and into the normal economic and social life of the community. I realize there is a transition period where it is a little difficult to know how to handle them and the hostel will undoubtedly do a good job.
It is so all-important, that is the point, and no money is being provided.

That is right; it is extremely important. This is a fairly recent development. I wish to assure the hon. member that I am keenly aware of the situation in that area and the Red Lake area in particular is one we have been watching very carefully. Of course, we run into difficulty there as both the hon. member and I remarked earlier this evening in deciding who is responsible for people who have for ten years been off the reservation.
Well, even for two.

I do not know whether these people are living in houses and paying municipal taxes and so on. They are certainly earning their livelihood in their communities and to all intents and purposes they are citizens of the municipalities. However, these are simply offhand remarks and are not intended to be an answer to the hon. member's question. We have taken a note of the other items on which he remarked and I shall see that he receives an answer to the specific points I have been unable to answer in my remarks this evening.

I wish to make one other observation and I think there is some advantage in doing so. The minister will be aware that there was recently held in Winnipeg what I believe is called a metis conference. Will the minister confirm that I have properly designated it?
If I am thinking of the same one it is called the greater Winnipeg council of social agencies or-
Welfare council?
-planning council or some such thing.

In Kenora, although not all people are interested in the problem of the integration of the Indians-and that is our difficulty-a sufficient number of people are interested that approximately 12 people at their own expense travelled 150 miles from Kenora to attend this conference in Winnipeg. Included among them were the recreational director, a couple of clergymen, an educator and a representative of the chamber of commerce. They attended the conference at their own expense. These people from Kenora are interested in the problem of trying to make the Indian welcome in the community. These are people that are farsighted enough to know that this is a problem that has to be dealt with.
Although 12 went to Winnipeg and profited from attending the conference those in Kenora who are interested in this matter are wondering whether it is possible to arrange in Kenora through the co-operation of the Indian affairs branch a conference which could be attended by responsible officials of the minister's department, chiefs of the bands that are contiguous to Kenora, and so on.

Of course, the particular conference to which the hon. member refers was not organized by my department but wherever a conference is organized under whatever auspices and where the question of the welfare of Indians is the subject of discussion, on invitation from the sponsoring authorities we always do send representatives-
You send good representatives.
-who are prepared to discuss the problems with which they may be confronted.
All the representatives of the minister's department are good.

I did not receive an answer from the minister about Mobert, Ontario. I asked a question about complaints received from the chief about welfare provisions as established within the agency and his inability to get people who are sick to hospital because of lack of funds and the difficulty of getting welfare assistance for young unmarried Indian males.
Again any matters affecting health come under the Department of National Health and Welfare. Was there any question apart from that of medical care?

Well, whose responsibility is it? Where does the chief take his complaints when he finds that the provisions for welfare and

health are not adequate? My own feeling is that he should not be taking them to his member of parliament. They should be taken to the Indian agent closest to him. I should like to know who is looking after the Mobert band.

I will be very glad to look into it, Mr. Chairman. I am not familiar offhand with the particular problem that is raised. As I said, any matters affecting health come under the jurisdiction of my colleague the Minister of National Health and Welfare. I should think the chief could take his problems to the Indian superintendent. I will be very glad to look into the matter and see what I can find out about it for the hon. member.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to direct a small question to the minister on a matter I raised last year concerning the housing project for the dominion Abitibi band reserve north of Amos. I understand that last year an amount was voted for a road or street development. I wonder whether there are any new developments and whether in the item for construction and acquisition we are about to vote there is an amount included for this housing project?

Mr. Chairman, I am afraid my officials have not come prepared with a breakdown of what is available on individual reserves. I can tell the hon. member that for the province of Quebec out of this total vote there is an amount of all purposes of $45,300 and $18,500 for agencies, but whether a part of that refers to what the hon. gentleman has just mentioned I could not say. However, I will look it up and let him know.

I think this will be my last question of the minister. In the last item to which I will not speak there is reference to education. The minister and I have been in correspondence. I pointed out that some of our senior Indian students were required to travel as far as 1,000 miles away from home if they wished to pursue their education at the high school level. In reply the minister reported to me that she had a plan for providing high school education for Indians at the lakehead. Has the plan progressed? Alternatively, could the minister tell me whether she thinks it would be cheaper, wiser and better to provide boarding allowances to high school students who might attend the local high schools in the communities nearest to them such as Fort Frances, Kenora or Sioux Lookout?

Mr. Chairman, of course we would like to have these students attend non-Indian schools. We think it is better in the long run to have the Indians take their
Supply-Labour
education and particularly their high school education in integrated schools. But once more may I say that I do not have the head of our education branch here.
I know the minister will write me and explain the matter.
Yes. I will do that.

May I take just one second before the vote carries, Mr. Chairman. I must say that I am rising to defend the minister. I wanted to say that I agree with the minister in her view that the Ontario government is not assuming its responsibilities in the matter of the education of these Indians who are not living on reserves. I did my best when I was minister to try to persuade them that Indians were citizens like other Canadians and that if they chose to live in a province and not on a reserve it was the business of the province to provide education for them as it did for other people. I am glad the minister took the same position tonight. I was rather hoping that one by-product of having a government of the political complexion of the present one was that the minister might have more influence at Queen's Park than I had. However, I am sorry that she has been obliged to confess the fact that she has no more influence than I had. If we both express in this House of Commons this view that the Ontario government ought to treat Indians as they treat other citizens, perhaps our voices may reach even to Queen's Park.
Mr. Dunlop said he would do it.

636. To carry out the purposes of the Technical and Vocational Training Assistance Act and agreements made thereunder-payments to the provinces-further amount required, $28,400,000.
