I assume that the minister has something to say on this item.

Mr. Chairman, this item in the further supplementary estimates for $28,400,000 is to provide additional funds for the fiscal year ending March 31, 1962, to meet our anticipated commitments under the Technical and Vocational Training Assistance Act.

Supply-Labour
A recent survey of the provinces indicated that claims made and to be submitted under the various programs provided for under the agreements for technical and vocational training assistance will now reach $75 million during the current fiscal year.
In the main estimates for 1961-62, the sum of $26,600,000 was provided: an additional $20 million was voted under item 534 of the supplementary estimates passed by the committee in September, 1961. This further sum of $28,400,000 is required to meet the claims expected as a result of the latest information we have now received from the provincial governments.
When we consider, Mr. Chairman, that federal payments for technical and vocational training during the past fiscal year, 1960-617, amounted in total to approximately $8,500,000, the committee will appreciate, I am sure, the rapid expansion which has taken place in the establishment of new training facilities under the new act.
Members of the committee will also appreciate from this large increase the major contribution which this government is making to meet the technical and vocational training needs across the country in co-operation with both provincial and local bodies.
Of the $75 million which I have mentioned, over $53 million will be paid this fiscal year for capital assistance to trade and vocational schools, technical institutions and vocational high schools or in other words to provide for training facilities.
Approval has been given so far under the agreements with the provinces for 245 projects. These cover the construction of 134 new schools, 80 major additions and 31 minor
additions to existing schools. These new facilities will provide for over 90,000 additional student placements.
It is obvious from the widespread response that the provincial and local authorities share the federal government's conviction that vigorous action is required to improve the technical knowledge and skill of our Canadian labour force.
It is this tremendous demand for new training facilities which has necessitated introducing this further supplemental estimate to provide for $28,400,000, in addition to the $46,600,000 in our original estimates.
The estimated total expenditure on the new projects is in excess of $269 million, of which the federal government's share will be about $179 million.
Included in these projects are the construction of one new institute of technology, 18 new trade schools, five new combined trade schools and institutes of technology and some 114 new vocational high schools.
Over and above these new schools, alterations and additions will be made to five institutes of technology, 16 trade schools, two combined trade schools and institutes, 56 vocational high schools and 31 minor alterations.
The total number of projects to date, the estimated expenditure for these new facilities, and the additional student accommodation by provinces, are as follows. I have here a table that I would ask permission of the committee to be included in Hansard.

It will contribute 50 per cent under our agreements with all of the ten provinces after this date.
This multi-million dollar federal-provincial program is a massive national effort to increase training facilities and programs. It has already far exceeded what we hoped would result when we introduced our training legislation to parliament in 1960.
The response of the provinces to our offer to pay 75 per cent of provincial expenditures for new training facilities until March 31, 1963, has been nothing short of remarkable. We had hoped to increase Canadian facilities by 50 per cent in a five year period, but it now appears that this goal will be met in less than half the time.
In addition to this expansion of training facilities, sparked by the new legislation, the agreements with the provincial governments provide assistance in various ways for the development and operation of training programs for both youth and adults. These programs include vocational high school training, technician training, trade and occupational training, training in industry, training of unemployed persons, training of disabled, training of technical and vocational teachers, vocational correspondence courses and student aid.
One of the main reasons for this program of greatly expanded assistance to technical and vocational training is the necessity for developing more highly skilled members of the labour force in response to automation and technological change.
The training programs now in operation are placing increased emphasis upon technical knowledge both of those now employed and for youth. Programs are also being promoted in industrial establishments to keep workers abreast of technological changes and to raise levels of basic skills.
Before closing, Mr. Chairman, I should like to explain briefly the composition of the item before us. By far the largest part of the total amount of $28,400,000 is required for capital assistance, namely, $24,550,000.
For technician training an amount of $3,341,300 is needed to provide for developments in this highly important area of training which were not foreseen when the original estimates were drawn up. The remaining amount of $508,700 is required, as explained in the estimates, to restore deductions made for anticipated lapses in the main estimates.
